learn.hook: You already 'know' Indian society: you have lived in it for 17 years. Sociology's first surprise is that this knowledge can be the very thing that stops you from seeing clearly.
points: This introductory chapter is non-evaluative in the CBSE 2026-27 syllabus, but its ideas run through the whole book.
Common-sense knowledge comes from socialisation: family, neighbourhood, school and media teach us what is 'normal'. It is real knowledge, but often partial and taken for granted.
Sociology asks us to unlearn: to set aside taken-for-granted ideas and look at familiar things as if seeing them for the first time.
Self-reflexivity is the ability to look at ourselves from the outside, as others might see us, and to question our own position and assumptions.

Sociology works like a social map: it shows where an individual stands in the wider landscape of groups, institutions and history. The book then covers demography, caste, tribe and family, inequality, cultural diversity and project work.

example.q: Meera, from a city family, says 'Everyone eats three meals at a table.' How would a self-reflexive sociologist respond?
steps: Notice that this is a common-sense belief learnt through her own socialisation.
Ask whose experience it reflects: her class, region and urban location.
Compare with other groups: farm workers, migrants, hostel students, families that sit on the floor.
Revise the claim after seeing her own position on the 'social map'.
example.answer: She treats her habit as one position among many, not as a universal fact. That is self-reflexivity.

learn.reallife: A Delhi student on an NSS camp in rural Odisha notices that 'normal' timings for meals, work and school are very different there. Questioning her own idea of 'normal' is the first step of sociology.

games.title: Match the idea
pairs: Seeing ourselves as others see us
Locating a person in the wider society
Learning norms from family, school and media

games.title: Common sense or sociology?
items: Common-sense knowledge about society is always wrong.
It is often partial or taken for granted, but not always wrong; sociology questions it rather than throwing it out.
Self-reflexivity means questioning our own assumptions and position.
It is the habit of looking at oneself from the outside.
Sociology can help a person see where they stand in relation to other groups.
That is the 'social map' idea.
Because we live in Indian society, we need no special effort to understand it.
Familiarity can hide things; sociology asks us to unlearn.
The introductory chapter of Indian Society is non-evaluative in CBSE 2026-27.
It is not examined, but sets up the book's ideas.

quiz.q: Students' existing knowledge of Indian society mainly comes from:
options: Socialisation in family, school and community
Formal sociological research projects in school
Official government census reports and tables
Studying the Constitution carefully in class
quiz.explain: We absorb most of what we 'know' about society from everyday socialisation.
quiz.mistake: Assumes everyday knowledge comes from formal study

quiz.q: Why does sociology ask students to 'unlearn'?
options: All earlier knowledge is false and must be thrown out
Taken-for-granted ideas can block a fresh, critical view
Textbooks must fully replace personal experience
Society never changes, so memory alone is enough
quiz.explain: Unlearning means questioning what we take for granted, not throwing away all experience.
quiz.mistake: Thinks unlearning means rejecting all prior knowledge

quiz.q: Self-reflexivity is best described as:
options: Seeing oneself as others might and questioning one's position
Quietly reflecting on nature and the natural environment
Faithfully adopting the views and values of one's elders
Studying the history of one's own family in detail
quiz.explain: Self-reflexivity turns the sociological gaze back on ourselves.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'reflexive' to mean simply thinking quietly

quiz.q: The 'social map' idea in sociology refers to:
options: A political map showing the states and districts of India
A census map showing population density by region
A list of a person's friends, relatives and contacts
Locating a person within the wider society and its history
quiz.explain: The map is metaphorical: it shows our place in society.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A student from a privileged background may not notice the advantages she enjoys.
Reason (R): Common-sense knowledge tends to reflect one's own social position.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Our 'common sense' is shaped by where we stand, so privilege can stay invisible to the privileged.
quiz.mistake: Misses the link between position and blind spots

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a theme of the later chapters of the book Indian Society?
options: Demographic structure
Caste, tribe and family
Challenges of cultural diversity
Planetary motion and gravitation
quiz.explain: The book covers demography, institutions, inequality and diversity, plus project work.
quiz.mistake: Guesses without recalling the book's outline

quiz.q: A city teenager says, 'Everyone has a smartphone these days.' A self-reflexive response would be to:
options: Agree, since it is clearly true in her colony
Ignore the statement as trivial and unimportant
Ask which groups she means, and who is left out
Suggest she compare phone prices online
quiz.explain: Self-reflexivity asks whose experience a claim describes.

quiz.q: Why is self-reflexivity especially important when studying one's own society?
options: Our own society has no biases
It replaces the need for evidence
It is needed only for studying foreign cultures
Familiarity makes our own biases harder to see
quiz.explain: We are inside our own society, so we must work harder to see it from outside.
quiz.mistake: Thinks reflexivity is only for unfamiliar cultures

teach.ask: Gappu flaps in: 'I already live in India, so why do I need sociology to understand it? What is this self-reflexivity thing?'
teach.praise: Ooh! So I must question my own 'normal' and see myself from outside. My feathers feel very reflexive now!
teach.nudge: But why can't I just trust what I already know? What do I need to unlearn?

topics.title: Colonialism and the making of modern India

learn.hook: The train you take to your nani's house runs on tracks first laid for carrying cotton and coal to the ports. Colonialism built modern India, but for its own purposes.
points: Modern Indian society, and Indians' awareness of themselves as a society, took shape in the context of colonial rule.
Colonialism unified India administratively and economically for the first time in a modern way, but this unification came through exploitation and domination.
Key colonial changes: railways and telegraph, a uniform legal and court system, new land revenue settlements, modern English education and a centralised bureaucracy.
The paradox of colonialism: it produced the very forces that opposed it. Western-educated Indians used ideas of liberty, rights and nationhood against British rule.
So colonialism was both a unifying and a dividing, both a modernising and an exploiting force.

example.q: How did railways show the double face of colonialism?
steps: Purpose: railways moved raw materials to ports and British goods inland, and helped move troops.
Effect: they also connected regions, allowed travel, pilgrimage and the spread of newspapers and ideas.
Result: Indians from distant regions could meet and organise, which helped nationalism.
example.answer: Built for colonial profit and control, railways also helped Indians see themselves as one people.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways still uses many 19th-century routes; today they carry crores of passengers, but their original map was drawn around colonial ports such as Bombay, Calcutta and Madras.

games.title: Unify or exploit?
items: A single administrative system across regions
Draining revenue to Britain
Railways linking distant provinces
Land revenue fixed to maximise collection
Common legal codes and courts
Raw materials shipped out for British industry

games.title: The colonial paradox
items: Colonialism produced Western-educated Indians who later led the nationalist movement.
This is the central paradox the chapter highlights.
Colonial unification of India happened through peaceful, equal partnership.
It happened through exploitation and domination.
Indian self-awareness as a society took shape partly under colonial rule.
Colonialism is the context of modern Indian self-awareness.
Colonial land revenue settlements had no lasting social effects.
They reshaped property rights and rural class relations.
Ideas of liberty learnt under colonial education were turned against colonial rule.
Nationalists used liberal ideas to expose colonial injustice.

quiz.q: In what context did modern Indian society and Indian self-awareness take shape?
options: The Mughal empire alone
Colonial rule
The Vedic age
Post-1991 liberalisation
quiz.explain: The chapter places the making of modern Indian society within colonialism.
quiz.mistake: Looks for an older or later period

quiz.q: Colonial unification of India was:
options: Real, but achieved through exploitation
Purely cultural, with no economic side
Voluntary and based on equal partnership
Entirely imaginary and without effect
quiz.explain: Administrative and economic unification happened, but at the cost of exploitation.
quiz.mistake: Treats unification as either fully good or not real

quiz.q: Which was a colonial administrative or economic change?
options: New land revenue settlements
The Panchayati Raj Act of 1992
The Green Revolution
The Five-Year Plans
quiz.explain: Land revenue settlements were introduced by the colonial state.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up colonial and post-independence policies

quiz.q: The 'paradox' of colonialism refers to the fact that:
options: It made India poorer and richer at exactly the same time
It ended in some provinces before it had even begun
It changed the economy but had no effect on society
It created forces, like educated nationalists, that opposed it
quiz.explain: Colonial education and unification helped produce the nationalism that ended colonial rule.
quiz.mistake: Misreads paradox as a simple contradiction in wealth

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Railways helped the growth of Indian nationalism.
Reason (R): The British built railways mainly to promote Indian self-rule.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Railways did help nationalism by connecting people, but they were built for colonial economic and military purposes.
quiz.mistake: Confuses an unintended effect with the purpose

quiz.q: Which group best illustrates how colonialism produced its own opponents?
options: European planters who ran tea estates in Assam
Western-educated Indians who led nationalist bodies
British civil servants posted in the provinces
Army officers sent out from Britain to India
quiz.explain: Indians trained in colonial schools used liberal ideas against the Raj.
quiz.mistake: Picks colonisers rather than the colonised

quiz.q: A uniform legal and court system under colonial rule is an example of:
options: Administrative unification
Deindustrialisation
Sanskritisation
Demographic transition
quiz.explain: A common legal framework helped bind regions into one administrative unit.
quiz.mistake: Confuses administrative change with other processes

quiz.q: Why does the book insist on studying colonialism to understand Indian society today?
options: Many present institutions and identities took shape under it
Colonial rule still formally continues in parts of India
Pre-colonial India had no real society or institutions
It is of purely historical interest, useful for examiners
quiz.explain: Railways, courts, education and even identities show colonial roots.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the past has no bearing on the present

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'If colonialism was so bad, how did it end up creating Indian nationalism? That's confusing!'
teach.praise: Wow, so colonialism tied India together to exploit it, and that very tying-together helped Indians resist. What a twist!
teach.nudge: But what exactly did colonialism change, and how did it accidentally help its opponents?

learn.hook: In 1885 a few dozen delegates met in Bombay; within decades, peasants, workers, students and women across the subcontinent were marching. How did so many different people come to feel like one nation?
points: Indian nationalism grew through the anti-colonial struggle; the shared experience of colonial domination helped people imagine India as one nation.
Under colonialism, communities based on caste, tribe, religion and region began to organise themselves in new ways, through associations, petitions and newspapers.
New classes emerged: an urban middle class of professionals, industrial workers, and peasants facing new revenue demands. Each organised around its own interests.
Reform movements (for example against sati or for women's education) and revival movements reshaped how communities saw themselves.
So nationalism coexisted with, and was shaped by, community and class identities, sometimes in harmony and sometimes in tension.

example.q: Give two kinds of identity, other than nation, that became organised in colonial India, with one example each.
steps: Community identity: caste associations petitioning for recognition, or religious reform bodies.
Class identity: industrial workers forming trade unions, or peasants protesting revenue demands.
Both used modern means such as print, meetings and petitions.
example.answer: Community (caste, tribe, religion, region) and class (middle class, workers, peasants) identities both organised.

learn.reallife: When you see a caste association's hall, a trade union office and a regional language newspaper in the same town today, you are seeing three kinds of collective identity that took modern shape in colonial times.

games.title: Community or class?
items: Caste association
Trade union of mill workers
Regional linguistic group
Peasants opposing high land revenue
Religious reform society
Urban professional middle class
Tribal group asserting its identity

items.text: Indian nationalism took shape through the ___ struggle.
options: anti-colonial
industrial
linguistic

items.text: Lawyers, teachers and clerks formed a new urban ___ class.
options: middle
ruling
landed
reform
peasant
labour

quiz.q: Indian nationalism developed mainly through:
options: Military conquest by one Indian kingdom
A single religious revival
The 1991 economic reforms
The shared struggle against colonial rule
quiz.explain: Common anti-colonial experience helped people imagine India as one nation.
quiz.mistake: Thinks nationalism came from one group's dominance

quiz.q: Which of these is a 'class' that emerged and organised in colonial India?
options: A jati
Industrial workers
A tribe
A linguistic region
quiz.explain: Workers are a class based on economic position; the others are community identities.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of community identity organising in colonial times?
options: A caste association submitting petitions
A chamber of commerce of British firms
A cricket club for officers
A railway timetable committee
quiz.explain: Caste associations were a new, modern way for communities to organise.

quiz.q: Reform and revival movements in colonial India:
options: Had no effect on identity
Were organised by the British government only
Reshaped how communities understood themselves
Were limited to economic demands
quiz.explain: Such movements reinterpreted traditions and community identities.
quiz.mistake: Underestimates the cultural role of reform

quiz.q: The new middle class of colonial India was largely made up of:
options: Large zamindars and their agents only
Labourers working on tea plantations
Hunter-gatherer communities of the forests
Western-educated lawyers, teachers and clerks
quiz.explain: Colonial education created a professional middle class.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the middle class with landed elites

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Nationalism and community identities in colonial India were always in perfect harmony.
Reason (R): Communities and classes organised around their own interests too.
options: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are false
quiz.explain: Since groups also pursued their own interests, nationalism sometimes faced tension with community and class claims.
quiz.mistake: Assumes unity meant no tension at all

quiz.q: Peasants protesting against high land revenue in colonial India were organising on the basis of:
options: Caste purity
Linguistic pride
Religious doctrine
Class interest
quiz.explain: Their shared economic position made it a class-based mobilisation.

quiz.q: Which means of organising became important for both communities and classes under colonialism?
options: Print media, public meetings and petitions
Royal court patronage only
Oral messages through village priests alone
Satellite television
quiz.explain: Modern communication allowed new forms of collective organisation.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How did people with so many castes, religions and regions start feeling like one Indian nation under the British?'
teach.praise: Got it! Fighting colonial rule together built the nation, while communities and classes organised in their own ways too.
teach.nudge: But who else was organising at that time, besides the nationalists?

chapters.title: Indian Society: The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society

topics.title: What demography studies, and the census

learn.hook: Every ten years, lakhs of enumerators knock on every door in India, from Ladakh to Lakshadweep, and ask the same questions. That giant headcount is the raw material of demography.
points: Demography is the systematic study of population: its size, composition (age, sex, literacy and so on), distribution over space, and change over time.

Formal demography is mathematical; it measures and forecasts population numbers. Social demography (population studies) looks at the social, economic and political causes and effects of population trends.
Demography grew alongside the modern nation-state and the science of statistics, because states wanted to count, plan for and govern their people. The census is its key data source.
In India, the first census attempts were made between 1867 and 1872; a regular census has been held every ten years since 1881. Independent India continued this decennial census from 1951.
Durkheim showed that suicide rates differ steadily between groups. Rates are therefore social facts: they reveal social patterns that individual stories cannot.

example.q: A researcher calculates that a district's population grew by 18 per cent in a decade; another asks why families there prefer sons. Which kind of demography is each doing?
steps: Calculating growth is measurement and counting.
So the first researcher is doing formal demography.
Asking about son preference looks at social causes and effects.
So the second researcher is doing social demography.
example.answer: First: formal demography. Second: social demography (population studies).

learn.reallife: Planning how many AIIMS-type hospitals, Kendriya Vidyalayas or ration shops a district needs starts with census figures on its population, age and literacy.

games.title: Match the term
pairs: Social causes and effects of population trends
Complete count of a country's people
A pattern, like a rate, that reveals society

games.title: Census history
items: First census attempts (1867-72)
Regular decennial census begins (1881)
First census of independent India (1951)
Census of 2011

quiz.q: Demography is the study of a population's:
options: Religious beliefs, practices and rituals only
Political party loyalties and voting patterns
Languages and dialects spoken, nothing else
Size, composition, distribution and change
quiz.explain: Demography covers all four aspects of population.
quiz.mistake: Thinks demography studies one narrow attribute

quiz.q: Which is an example of social demography?
options: Projecting the 2041 population by formula
Studying why some families prefer sons
Computing a crude birth rate
Tabulating census totals by age
quiz.explain: Social demography asks about social causes and consequences.

quiz.q: Why did demography develop along with the modern nation-state?
options: Kings had always wanted to count only their soldiers
States needed data to plan for and govern their people
It was required by the rules of world trade bodies
It began only after computers and the internet
quiz.explain: Counting the population helped modern states plan and administer.
quiz.mistake: Misses the link with state planning

quiz.q: Since which year has India held a regular census every ten years?
quiz.explain: First attempts were made in 1867-72; the regular decennial census began in 1881.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the first attempts or the first post-independence census with the start of the regular series

quiz.q: The first census of independent India was held in:
quiz.explain: The decennial series continued after independence, with 1951 as the first.

quiz.q: Durkheim's study of suicide rates shows that:
options: Suicide is purely a matter of private, personal choice
Rates are of no real use to sociologists at all
Only psychologists can study suicide in a proper way
Rates can reveal social patterns beyond individual motives
quiz.explain: Stable differences in rates between groups point to social causes.
quiz.mistake: Treats the rate as a sum of private decisions

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The census is a key source for demography.
Reason (R): It counts the whole population and records age, sex, literacy and more.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Because it covers everyone and many attributes, the census is the backbone of population data.
quiz.mistake: Fails to see why the census is so useful

quiz.q: A table showing that a state's population rose from 5 crore to 6 crore is most useful for:
options: Formal demography
Social stratification theory
Kinship studies
Religious studies
quiz.explain: Counting and measuring change is the work of formal demography.
quiz.mistake: Confuses demographic data with other branches

teach.ask: Gappu peeps at a census form: 'Why does the government count everybody? And what's the difference between formal and social demography?'
teach.praise: Ah, formal demography counts and calculates, social demography asks why. And the census gives them both the numbers!
teach.nudge: But what exactly does demography study, and how does social demography differ from just counting?

learn.hook: In 1798 an English clergyman predicted that humanity would always outrun its food. More than two centuries later, the world has more people than ever, and far more food. What did Malthus miss?
points: Thomas Robert Malthus argued that population grows in a geometric progression (2, 4, 8, 16...) while food supply grows only in an arithmetic progression (1, 2, 3, 4...).
So population would always press on food, keeping most people near subsistence. Prosperity could only be secured by controlling population growth.
Positive checks are natural ones that raise deaths: famines, diseases and wars. Preventive checks are human choices that lower births: late marriage, celibacy and sexual abstinence.

Criticisms: European history showed population and living standards both rising; technology greatly raised food output. Liberal and Marxist scholars argued poverty comes from unequal distribution of resources, not from population itself.

example.q: Starting with population 2 units and food 1 unit, and doubling population while food rises by 1 unit each period, what are the values after three more periods?
steps: Population: 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 (geometric).
Food: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 (arithmetic).
Population per unit of food: 16 / 4 = 4, up from 2.
example.answer: Population 16, food 4: the gap widens, which is Malthus's warning.

learn.reallife: India went from food imports in the 1960s to large grain buffer stocks in FCI godowns after the Green Revolution, even as population kept rising, a real-life challenge to Malthus.

games.title: Positive or preventive check?
items: Famine
Epidemic disease
War
Late marriage
Celibacy
Sexual abstinence

games.title: Was Malthus right?
items: Malthus said food supply grows geometrically.
He said food grows arithmetically and population geometrically.
Rising farm technology weakened Malthus's prediction.
Food output rose much faster than he expected.
Liberal and Marxist critics blamed poverty on unequal distribution of resources.
They argued poverty is caused by inequality, not population alone.
Late marriage is a positive check in Malthus's theory.
It is a preventive check, a human choice that lowers births.
In Europe, population and living standards rose together after the 19th century.
Historical evidence went against Malthus.

quiz.q: According to Malthus, population increases in a:
options: Arithmetic progression
Constant, fixed rate
Random pattern
Geometric progression
quiz.explain: Malthus: population 2, 4, 8, 16; food 1, 2, 3, 4.

quiz.q: Which is a 'positive check' in Malthus's theory?
options: Famine
Late marriage
Celibacy
Abstinence
quiz.explain: Positive checks raise deaths: famines, diseases, wars.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'positive' means a good, voluntary check

quiz.q: Which is a 'preventive check' in Malthus's theory?
options: War
Late marriage
Epidemic disease
Famine
quiz.explain: Preventive checks lower births by human choice.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two types of checks

quiz.q: If population doubles each generation from 3 crore, what will it be after 3 generations of geometric growth (in crore)?
quiz.explain: 3 → 6 → 12 → 24: doubling three times multiplies by 8.
steps: Generation 1: 3 × 2 = 6
Generation 2: 6 × 2 = 12
Generation 3: 12 × 2 = 24
quiz.mistake: Adds 3 each time (arithmetic) or doubles only twice

quiz.q: Which historical evidence went against Malthus?
options: European population and living standards rose together
European population stopped growing after about 1800
Food output in Europe fell steadily after 1850
Famines increased everywhere in Europe after 1850
quiz.explain: Rising food output and incomes alongside growing population contradicted him.

quiz.q: Liberal and Marxist critics argued that poverty and starvation are caused mainly by:
options: Too many children being born in every family
Lack of effort and laziness among the poor
Bad weather and failed monsoons alone
Unequal distribution of economic resources
quiz.explain: They shifted the focus from numbers to inequality.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Malthus believed prosperity required controlling population growth.
Reason (R): He thought food supply could never keep up with unchecked population growth.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Because food lagged behind population, he saw population control as the key to prosperity.

quiz.q: What was one key factor Malthus underestimated?
options: The effect of wars on the number of deaths
The power of technology to raise food output
The role of epidemic disease in history
People's willingness to marry at a young age
quiz.explain: Agricultural technology raised food supply far beyond arithmetic growth.
quiz.mistake: Picks something central to his own theory

teach.ask: Gappu worries: 'Malthus says we'll all run out of food! Should I stop eating grains?'
teach.praise: Phew! So Malthus feared population would outrun food, but technology and fairer distribution proved him wrong. I'll keep my grains!
teach.nudge: But how fast did Malthus think population and food grow, and why do critics say he was wrong?

learn.hook: Imagine a village where vaccines arrive overnight but ideas about family size change only over decades. Births stay high, deaths crash, and the population shoots up. That gap is the heart of demographic transition.
points: The theory of demographic transition links population growth to the overall level of economic development. Each society passes through typical stages.
Stage 1: underdeveloped, technologically backward society; high birth rate and high death rate, so slow growth.
Stage 2 (transition): death rate falls sharply with better medicine, food and sanitation, but birth rate stays high. The result is very rapid growth, the 'population explosion'.
Stage 3: developed society; low birth rate and low death rate, so slow growth again.
Why the lag? Death rates can be brought down quickly by technology (vaccines, clean water), while birth rates depend on deep socio-cultural norms about marriage and family that change slowly.

example.q: A country has birth rate 40 and death rate 38 per 1000. Twenty years later birth rate is 38 and death rate is 15. Which stages are these and what happened?
steps: First period: both high, natural increase 40 − 38 = 2 per 1000: Stage 1.
Later: death rate fell sharply, birth rate barely moved; natural increase 38 − 15 = 23 per 1000.
Rapid growth with falling deaths and high births is Stage 2, the transition.
example.answer: It moved from Stage 1 to Stage 2: a population explosion caused by falling mortality.

learn.reallife: India's population explosion between 1951 and 1981 followed exactly this pattern: malaria and smallpox control cut deaths quickly, while birth rates fell much more slowly.

games.title: Stages of demographic transition
items: High birth and high death rates, slow growth
Death rate falls while birth rate stays high
Rapid growth: population explosion
Low birth and low death rates, slow growth

games.title: Changes fast or slowly?
items: Vaccination drives
Clean drinking water
Control of epidemics
Norms about ideal family size
Age at marriage
Value placed on sons

quiz.q: The theory of demographic transition links population growth to:
options: The main religion followed in a society
The level of economic development
The size of a country's standing army
Climate and rainfall, and nothing else
quiz.explain: Each stage corresponds to a level of development.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the theory is about culture or geography only

quiz.q: Which stage of demographic transition shows a 'population explosion'?
options: The first stage, with high birth rates and high death rates
The final stage, with low birth rates and low death rates
The transitional stage, with falling deaths and high births
No particular stage; such explosions are random events
quiz.explain: The gap between falling death rates and high birth rates causes rapid growth.
quiz.mistake: Picks the stage with the highest rates

quiz.q: In the first stage of demographic transition, population grows slowly because:
options: Both birth and death rates are low
Birth rate is low and death rate high
Migration is very high
Both birth and death rates are high
quiz.explain: High births are cancelled out by high deaths.
quiz.mistake: Assumes slow growth always means low birth rate

quiz.q: Why do death rates usually fall faster than birth rates?
options: People generally prefer more deaths than more births
Birth rates are fixed by law and so can never change
Medicine cuts deaths fast; fertility norms change slowly
Death rates depend only on the climate and the season
quiz.explain: Technology acts quickly on mortality; fertility is rooted in social attitudes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks births and deaths respond equally to technology

quiz.q: A country has a birth rate of 36 and a death rate of 12 per 1000. What is its rate of natural increase per 1000?
quiz.explain: Natural increase = birth rate − death rate = 36 − 12 = 24 per 1000.
steps: Natural increase = BR − DR
quiz.mistake: Adds the rates, divides them, or reports the death rate

quiz.q: A developed country with low birth and low death rates is in which stage?
options: First stage
Second stage
Pre-transition stage
Third stage
quiz.explain: Low birth and death rates mark the final stage.
quiz.mistake: Confuses slow growth of stage 1 and stage 3

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Population explosion happens in the transitional stage.
Reason (R): In this stage, the birth rate falls faster than the death rate.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are false
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: The explosion happens because the death rate falls faster while the birth rate stays high; R reverses this.

quiz.q: Both Stage 1 and Stage 3 show slow growth. What is the key difference?
options: Stage 1 has high birth and death rates; Stage 3 has low ones
Stage 1 has low birth and death rates; Stage 3 high ones
There is no difference at all between the two
Stage 3 has negative growth while Stage 1 has none
quiz.explain: Slow growth can come from high-high or low-low rates.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the same growth means the same rates

teach.ask: Gappu squawks: 'If doctors save more lives, why does the population suddenly explode? Shouldn't that be good news only?'
teach.praise: So when deaths fall quickly but births stay high for a while, the population zooms up. That's the transition stage!
teach.nudge: But what happens to birth rates and death rates in each stage, and which one changes first?

learn.hook: If a city of 20 lakh records 44,000 births in a year, is that a lot? Demographers turn raw counts into rates so we can compare Kerala with Bihar or 1951 with 2011.
points: Birth rate (crude birth rate): number of live births per 1000 population in a given area in a year. Death rate: number of deaths per 1000 population per year.
Rate of natural increase (growth rate) = birth rate − death rate (ignoring migration). When it is close to zero, the population has reached replacement level.
Fertility rate: number of live births per 1000 women in the child-bearing age group, usually 15 to 49 years.
Total fertility rate (TFR): the average number of children a woman would bear over her lifetime if she followed current age-specific fertility rates.
Replacement-level TFR is about 2.1 children per woman; the extra 0.1 allows for children who die before reaching reproductive age.

example.q: A town of 2,00,000 people records 4,800 live births and 1,400 deaths in a year. Find the birth rate, death rate and rate of natural increase.
steps: Natural increase = 24 − 7 = 17 per 1000, i.e. 1.7 per cent.
example.answer: Birth rate 24, death rate 7, natural increase 17 per 1000.

learn.reallife: Health officers in Kerala and Uttar Pradesh compare TFRs from the Sample Registration System to decide where to focus family-welfare camps and ASHA workers.

steps: Birth rate = births / population × 1000

quiz.q: A state has a birth rate of 19 and a death rate of 7 per 1000. What is its rate of natural increase in per cent?
quiz.explain: Natural increase = 19 − 7 = 12 per 1000 = 1.2 per cent.
quiz.mistake: Leaves the answer per 1000 or adds the rates

options: Women aged 15 to 49 years

quiz.explain: Fertility rate uses women of child-bearing age as the base.
quiz.mistake: Confuses fertility rate with crude birth rate

quiz.explain: Fertility rate = 200 / 2500 × 1000 = 80.
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong base or forgets ×1000

quiz.q: Replacement-level total fertility rate is about:
quiz.explain: About 2.1 children per woman replace both parents, allowing for some child deaths.
quiz.mistake: Thinks exactly 2.0 or a large number is needed

options: Total number of births in a country per year
Number of births per 1000 people in a year
Average number of children a woman would bear
Number of women who give birth in a year
quiz.explain: TFR is a lifetime average per woman, based on current fertility rates.

quiz.q: When the rate of natural increase is close to zero, the population is said to have reached:
options: Population explosion
Replacement level
Demographic dividend
Stage two of transition
quiz.explain: Births just balance deaths, so the population replaces itself.

quiz.q:

Reason (R): Some children die before they reach reproductive age.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: The extra 0.1 compensates for child mortality.
quiz.mistake: Misses why the figure is not exactly 2

teach.ask: Gappu holds a calculator: 'How do I find a birth rate, and what is this TFR of 2.1 everyone talks about?'
teach.praise: Births per 1000 people, minus deaths per 1000, gives natural increase. And 2.1 children per woman keeps the population steady. Numbers are fun!
teach.nudge: But how do I turn a count of births into a rate, and what does replacement level mean?

topics.title: Infant and maternal mortality, life expectancy and sex ratio

learn.hook: A falling infant mortality rate is one of the most sensitive signs of a nation's health. It reflects mothers' nutrition, clean water, vaccines and the reach of public health centres.
points: Infant mortality rate (IMR): number of deaths of babies before the age of one year per 1000 live births.
Maternal mortality rate (MMR): number of women who die in childbirth per 1,00,000 live births.
Low IMR and MMR indicate good health care, nutrition and economic development.
Life expectancy: the estimated number of years an average person is expected to survive, based on age-specific death rates. It rises as health and living conditions improve.
Sex ratio: number of females per 1000 males in a given area at a given time (India's convention). Below 1000 means fewer females than males.

example.q: In a state, 80,000 live births took place in a year; 2,400 babies died before their first birthday and 96 mothers died in childbirth. Find IMR and MMR.
steps: IMR = 2400 / 80000 × 1000 = 30 per 1000 live births.
example.answer: IMR = 30; MMR = 120.

learn.reallife: Institutional deliveries under Janani Suraksha Yojana and immunisation drives have helped reduce India's IMR and MMR, especially in rural districts.

games.title: Match each measure to its base
pairs: Average years a person is expected to live

1000 population

quiz.explain: IMR uses live births as the base, per 1000.
quiz.mistake: Uses total population or the MMR base

quiz.explain: Because maternal deaths are rarer, the base is 1,00,000 live births.

quiz.explain: Sex ratio = 47000 / 50000 × 1000 = 940 females per 1000 males.

options: Estimated average years a person is expected to live

quiz.explain: It is an estimate based on age-specific death rates.
quiz.mistake: Confuses life expectancy with the oldest age or average age

quiz.q: A sex ratio of 1084 in a district means:
options: There are more females than males

quiz.explain: Above 1000 means more than 1000 females per 1000 males.
quiz.mistake: Reads the Indian sex ratio as males per females

quiz.q:

Reason (R): Infant survival depends on nutrition, sanitation and medical care.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: Since infant survival depends on these conditions, IMR reflects development.

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'What are IMR and MMR, and how do you calculate a sex ratio?'
teach.praise: IMR is baby deaths per 1000 live births, MMR is mothers' deaths per 1,00,000 live births, and sex ratio is females per 1000 males. Got it!
teach.nudge: But what is the base for each of these measures? Per 1000 of what?

topics.title: Age structure, dependency and the demographic dividend

learn.hook: India is one of the youngest large countries in the world. Crores of young people could power its startups and factories, or swell the queues at employment exchanges. Which one happens depends on choices made now.
points: Age structure is the proportion of people in different age groups. An age pyramid shows it: a wide base means many children; a narrow base and wider top mean an ageing population.
Dependency ratio = (population below 15 + population above 64) ÷ population aged 15-64, often × 100. A falling ratio means relatively more working-age people.
Demographic dividend: the economic advantage of a large working-age share. It is gained only if the young get education, skills and jobs; otherwise it becomes a burden of youth unemployment.
In India, the 0-14 share has been falling and the 15-59 share rising; the 60+ share is slowly growing. Kerala's pyramid is older (more aged people), Uttar Pradesh's is younger (more children).
Population momentum: even after fertility falls, population keeps growing for decades because large young cohorts are entering child-bearing ages.

example.q: A region has 3,000 children under 15, 600 people over 64 and 6,000 people aged 15-64. Find the dependency ratio.
steps: Dependants = 3000 + 600 = 3600.
Working-age = 6000.
Dependency ratio = 3600 / 6000 × 100 = 60.
example.answer: 60 dependants per 100 working-age people.

learn.reallife: Skill India and the many engineering, ITI and nursing institutes are attempts to turn India's large youth population into a demographic dividend rather than a jobless crowd.

quiz.explain: More elderly people add to the numerator of the dependency ratio.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the elderly are dependants

quiz.q: In India over recent decades, the share of the 0-14 age group has been:

quiz.explain: Falling fertility shrinks the youngest share while the working-age share grows.
quiz.mistake: Assumes India's population is getting younger

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'Everyone says India's young population is a dividend. Is that a gift that comes automatically?'
teach.praise: Ah, a big working-age share lowers dependency and can be a dividend, but only with education and jobs. No free gifts!
teach.nudge: But what does the dependency ratio measure, and what conditions turn young people into a dividend?

topics.title: India's population growth and the fall in death rates

learn.hook: Between 1911 and 1921, India's population actually shrank. Between 1951 and 1981 it grew faster than ever before. The story behind these two decades is a story of epidemics, famines and medicine.
points: India's population grew from about 23.8 crore in 1901 to about 121 crore in 2011. Growth was slow until 1921.
1911-21 saw negative growth, mainly because the influenza epidemic of 1918-19 killed millions.
After 1921, and especially in 1951-81, growth was rapid (over 2 per cent a year at its peak) because the death rate fell sharply while the birth rate stayed high.
Death rates fell through control of famines and of epidemic diseases such as plague, smallpox and cholera, plus vaccination, better sanitation and medical care.

Amartya Sen showed famines are caused by a 'failure of entitlements': people lack the means to buy food, not only because food is scarce. Poverty, poor transport and state inaction worsened famines; employment schemes such as MGNREGA (2005) aim to protect rural livelihoods.

example.q: A table shows India's annual growth rate: 1901-11: 0.56%, 1911-21: −0.03%, 1951-61: 1.96%, 1961-71: 2.20%. What conclusions follow?
steps: 1911-21 is negative: population actually fell (influenza epidemic).
Growth jumped after independence, above 2 per cent in 1961-71.
The jump reflects falling death rates while birth rates stayed high.
example.answer: Growth was slow and briefly negative early on, then rose sharply after 1951 as mortality fell.

learn.reallife: The smallpox eradication campaign and the near-elimination of famine deaths after 1947 are big reasons India's population grew so fast in the mid-20th century.

quiz.explain: It was about 238 million (23.8 crore) in 1901.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why did India's population suddenly race ahead after independence? And why did it shrink once?'
teach.praise: Influenza made the population shrink in 1911-21, and after 1951 falling deaths with high births made it race ahead. History in numbers!
teach.nudge: But what made deaths fall so fast, and what happened in 1911-21?

topics.title: Why birth rates fall slowly: regional fertility differences

learn.hook: Kerala and Tamil Nadu reached replacement fertility while some northern states still had TFRs well above 3. Same country, same national policy. Why such different results?
points: Birth rates fall slowly because fertility is a socio-cultural matter: age at marriage, value of children for labour and old-age support, son preference and women's status all play a role.
Falling death rates can come quickly through technology, but family-size norms change over generations.
States like Kerala and Tamil Nadu reached replacement-level fertility; others such as Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, West Bengal, Maharashtra and Karnataka are close to it.
States like Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan have had higher TFRs, so they will account for a large share of India's future growth.
Low fertility usually goes with high female literacy, better health care, later marriage and women's greater say in decisions.

example.q: Why might a state with high female literacy have lower fertility?
steps: Educated women tend to marry later.
They are more aware of contraception and health care, and child survival is higher.
They have more say in family decisions and more work outside the home.
example.answer: Female education delays marriage, improves child survival and empowers women, all of which lower fertility.

learn.reallife: ASHA workers in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh focus on delaying marriage and spacing births, the same social changes that earlier lowered fertility in Kerala.

quiz.explain: The wish for a son can push families beyond their intended size.

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: 'Same India, same laws, so why is fertility so low in Kerala and higher in Bihar?'
teach.praise: So fertility follows social change like women's education and later marriage, which is why Kerala and Tamil Nadu got there first!
teach.nudge: But what social factors make birth rates fall, and which states show low or high fertility?

learn.hook: Biology alone would give slightly more girls than boys in a healthy population, because women tend to live longer. Yet India's sex ratio fell for most of the 20th century. Something social is going on.
points: India's sex ratio declined through the 20th century: about 972 females per 1000 males in 1901 to 927 in 1991, with a small recovery to 933 in 2001.
The child sex ratio (age 0-6) has fallen faster: from 945 in 1991 to 927 in 2001, and lower still in 2011. This points to bias at birth and in early childhood.
Reasons: son preference, neglect of girl children (in food and medical care), female infanticide, and sex-selective abortion made possible by ultrasound technology.
The lowest child sex ratios are found in prosperous regions such as Punjab, Haryana and Delhi, showing that prosperity alone does not remove bias; it can even fund sex selection.
The PNDT Act of 1994 (amended in 2003 as the PCPNDT Act) bans sex determination; Beti Bachao Beti Padhao promotes the value of daughters. Laws help, but lasting change needs changed social attitudes.

example.q: A district's child sex ratio is 850 while its overall sex ratio is 930. What does this gap suggest?
steps: The child ratio covers only ages 0-6, i.e. recent births.
A much lower child ratio means fewer girls are being born or surviving in recent years.
That points to sex-selective abortion or neglect of girl infants.
example.answer: Bias against girls has worsened recently, concentrated at birth and early childhood.

learn.reallife: Many districts in Haryana improved their child sex ratio after strict PCPNDT enforcement and Beti Bachao Beti Padhao campaigns, though change in attitudes remains the real goal.

teach.ask: Gappu looks puzzled: 'Why does India have fewer girls than boys, when nature should give slightly more females?'
teach.praise: So son preference, neglect and sex selection, even in rich regions, pulled the ratio down. Laws help, but attitudes must change. Hooray for daughters!
teach.nudge: But what social practices are causing the decline, and what has the state done about it?

learn.hook: In 1951 fewer than one in five Indians could read; by 2011 about three in four could. Meanwhile crores of people moved from village to city, some for wages, some to escape caste oppression.
points: Literacy empowers people: it opens jobs, awareness and choices, and it is linked to better health and lower fertility, especially female literacy.
Literacy rose from about 18 per cent in 1951 to about 74 per cent in 2011, but a gender gap remains: female literacy is well below male literacy.
Literacy varies by region (Kerala very high, Bihar much lower) and by social group (Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes have lower literacy, especially among women).
About two-thirds of Indians (nearly 69 per cent in 2011) still live in villages, but the urban share is rising. Agriculture's share in GDP has fallen sharply, though many people still depend on it.

Push factors: lack of rural work, decline of common property resources (ponds, forests, grazing lands), and the need for cash. Pull factors: urban jobs and anonymity, which can free lower castes from rural caste oppression. Mass media also carries urban lifestyles into villages.

example.q: Classify the reasons for Ramesh's move from his village to Surat: (a) his village pond and grazing land were taken over; (b) Surat's textile mills offer wages; (c) in the city nobody asks his caste.
steps: (a) Decline of common property resources is a push factor.
(b) Urban jobs are a pull factor.
(c) Anonymity of city life is a pull factor.
example.answer: (a) push; (b) and (c) pull.

learn.reallife: Construction sites in Bengaluru and Mumbai are full of migrants from Odisha, Bihar and Jharkhand, pushed by lack of farm work and pulled by daily wages.

learn.hook: India launched a national family planning programme in 1952, among the first countries in the world to do so. Its journey, including one dark chapter, shows what states can and cannot do about population.
points: The National Family Planning Programme began in 1952. Its objective was to influence the rate and pattern of population growth in socially desirable directions.
Methods included birth control (contraception and sterilisation), improving public health and spreading awareness.
During the Emergency (1975-76) the programme turned coercive: mass sterilisation drives with targets, often forced on poor men, caused a strong public backlash.
After the Emergency it was renamed the National Family Welfare Programme, with a non-coercive approach linking population to maternal and child health and wider welfare.

The National Population Policy 2000 and the National Health Policy 2017 set goals such as reaching replacement-level TFR (2.1) and lowering infant and maternal mortality. The lesson: the state can create conditions, but fertility falls with social and economic change.

example.q: Why did coercive sterilisation during the Emergency backfire?
steps: Targets led officials to force sterilisation on poor and vulnerable people.
This violated consent and created fear and anger.
Public backlash made family planning politically unpopular for years.
example.answer: Coercion destroyed trust; later policy shifted to voluntary, welfare-based approaches.

learn.reallife: Today's health and family-welfare schemes stress choice: spacing methods, counselling by ASHAs and maternal health care, rather than targets.

teach.nudge: But what went wrong during the Emergency, and how did policy change afterwards?

chapters.title: Indian Society: Social Institutions: Continuity and Change

topics.title: Caste: varna, jati and its features

learn.hook: Caste, tribe and family are institutions you were born into without being asked. This chapter shows how each has stayed the same in some ways and changed in others. We begin with caste, a word that is not even Indian in origin.
points: Caste, tribe and family are key institutions of Indian society; each shows both continuity and change.
The English word 'caste' comes from the Portuguese 'casta' (pure breed). It is used for two Indian terms: varna and jati.
Varna (literally 'colour') is the fourfold all-India classification: Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra, with a large group outside it, the 'outcastes' or untouchables (ati-shudra).
Jati is a generic term for species or kinds; jatis are local, regionally variable groups and are the real working units of caste. There are thousands of them.

Features: membership by birth; endogamy (marriage within the group); rules about food and sharing food; a hierarchy of rank; segmental sub-divisions (sub-castes); traditional link with hereditary occupations. Caste was less rigid in the early Vedic period and became rigid later.

example.q: A woman cannot change her jati by moving to another town, earning more or marrying outside. Which features of caste does this show?
steps: She was assigned her caste at birth: membership by birth.
Marriage is expected within the group: endogamy.
Earnings do not change caste rank: caste is ascribed, not achieved.
example.answer: Ascription by birth and endogamy, the two core features.

learn.reallife: Matrimonial columns that still specify caste show how endogamy, one of caste's oldest features, continues even in tech-savvy apps and newspapers.

quiz.explain: Endogamy is marriage inside the group.

options: Ranking of castes by wealth only

quiz.explain: Castes are divided into sub-castes and sometimes further.

options: Link with hereditary occupation

quiz.explain: Caste membership is fixed at birth.

quiz.q:

Reason (R): One is born into one's caste and cannot normally change it.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: Ascribed status is given at birth, which is exactly how caste works.

quiz.q: Historically, caste distinctions were:
options: Less rigid in the early Vedic period than later
Most rigid in the early Vedic period
Unchanged since the very earliest times
Created for the first time under colonial rule
quiz.explain: Caste rigidity increased in the post-Vedic period.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Is caste the same as varna? And what makes caste different from just being in a club?'
teach.praise: So varna is the fourfold scheme, jati is the real local group, and you're born into it and marry within it. Not a club at all!
teach.nudge: But how are varna and jati different, and what are caste's main features?

topics.title: Separation and hierarchy: caste's two principles

learn.hook: Caste works like two rules running at once: keep groups apart, and arrange them in a ladder. Together they create a system that is both divided and whole.
points: Principle 1, difference and separation: each caste is supposed to be different from and separate from others, through rules on marriage, food, social interaction and occupation.
Principle 2, wholeness and hierarchy: the separated castes are not equal; they fit into a hierarchical whole, like parts of a body, each with its place.
The hierarchy is based on the distinction between 'purity' and 'pollution': castes considered ritually pure are ranked higher, those considered impure lower.
In theory ritual status and material (economic, political) status could be separate. In practice they usually coincided: upper castes tended to hold land and power, lower castes tended to be poor.

example.q: Explain how rules about who may cook for whom express both principles of caste.
steps: Separation: castes keep apart by not sharing cooked food freely.
Hierarchy: food usually flows from higher to lower, not the reverse, because of purity rules.
So one practice both divides groups and ranks them.
example.answer: Food rules separate castes and rank them by purity and pollution.

learn.reallife: Practices like separate utensils for some guests, still reported in surveys in parts of India, show how ideas of purity and pollution can linger in daily life.

options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A

quiz.explain: The coincidence of ritual and material status explains upper-caste economic power.
quiz.mistake: Misses the overlap of caste and class

teach.ask: Gappu twitters: 'If castes are kept separate, how can they also be part of one system?'
teach.praise: Separate but stacked! Castes are kept apart and also ranked in one whole by purity and pollution.
teach.nudge: But what are the two principles, and what is the hierarchy based on?

learn.hook: When British officials tried to count and rank every caste in the 1901 census, thousands of petitions arrived demanding a higher place. Counting caste changed caste.
points: Colonial rulers tried to understand Indian society in order to govern it. Systematic enumeration of caste began with the census.

The 1901 census, under Herbert Risley, tried to collect information on the social hierarchy of castes, i.e. their order of social precedence in each region. This made caste identities more rigid and sparked petitions from castes claiming higher status.
Colonial land revenue settlements and related laws gave legal recognition to the customary rights of upper castes, turning them into owners of land in the modern sense.

The Government of India Act, 1935 gave legal recognition to lists or 'schedules' of castes and tribes marked out for special treatment by the state, origin of the terms Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
So colonialism did not invent caste, but it changed it, making it more rigid and more a matter of official identity.

example.q: How did the act of counting caste in the census change caste itself?
steps: The census asked people to fit into fixed, named caste categories.
In 1901 it also tried to rank castes in a hierarchy.
Castes organised and petitioned for higher rank.
Caste became more rigid and politically important.
example.answer: Official counting froze fluid identities and made caste a matter of state record and competition.

learn.reallife: When state governments today ask for a caste-wise survey, the debate echoes the colonial census: counting categories can shape the identities being counted.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Did the British create caste? What did they actually do to it?'

teach.nudge: But which colonial measures affected caste, and how?

topics.title: Caste in the present: reform, the state and change

learn.hook: In a metro train, nobody asks your caste before you sit down. But at a wedding, caste often still decides who marries whom. Modern India changed caste in public life far more than in private life.
points: Opposition to caste came from reformers and nationalists: Jyotiba Phule, B.R. Ambedkar and Mahatma Gandhi (in different ways) attacked untouchability and caste discrimination. Abolishing caste was part of the nationalist programme.
The independent state was committed to abolishing caste, yet it also used caste as a basis for reservations to undo historical injustice. This is a contradiction the book highlights.
Industrialisation, urbanisation and education weakened caste rules in public life: factory and office jobs, eating in restaurants and travelling in trains and buses made strict separation hard.
In the cultural and domestic sphere caste has proved resilient, especially endogamy: most marriages still take place within the caste.

example.q: Why does the book call the state's approach to caste 'contradictory'?
steps: The state aimed for a caste-free society.
But to correct past injustice it used caste to define who gets reservations.
So it both sought to abolish caste and gave caste an official role.
example.answer: It wanted to end caste but had to recognise caste to remedy caste-based disadvantage.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways never had caste-wise coaches, and urban offices hire by qualification; yet marriage portals still offer filters by caste. Public change, private continuity.

quiz.q: Which statement about caste today is most accurate?
options: It has disappeared from every sphere of Indian life

quiz.explain: Change has been uneven across public and private spheres.

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'Has caste disappeared in modern India? I see people mixing everywhere in the city!'
teach.praise: So caste weakened in trains, offices and restaurants, but endogamy keeps it alive at home. And the state both opposes and uses caste. Tricky!
teach.nudge: But where has caste weakened and where does it still persist?

topics.title: Caste and politics: dominant castes and visibility

learn.hook: At election time, analysts on TV talk about caste 'arithmetic' in every constituency. Democracy did not end caste; it gave caste a new job.
points: Caste became a basis for political mobilisation: caste associations formed, parties built caste-based support bases or 'vote banks', and castes acted as pressure groups.

M.N. Srinivas's 'dominant castes': castes that are numerically large, own land and hold political power in a region. Many were middle castes that gained from land reforms, e.g. Yadavs (Bihar, UP), Vokkaligas (Karnataka), Reddys and Kammas (Andhra Pradesh), Marathas (Maharashtra), Jats (Punjab, Haryana, western UP) and Patidars (Gujarat).
Sanskritisation, adopting the customs of higher castes, was one route by which castes sought upward mobility.
For urban upper castes caste has become 'invisible': having gained economic and educational capital from caste in the past, they can now claim to be 'caste-less' and rely on merit.
For SC, ST and OBC groups caste has become hyper-visible, because their caste identity is central to claims on reservations and other state protection.

example.q: An urban professional says, 'Caste doesn't matter to me at all.' A villager from a Scheduled Caste says caste shapes everything in his life. How does the book explain both views?
steps: The professional's family may have built education and wealth through past caste privilege.
Now that capital passes on without visible caste help, caste looks 'invisible' to him.
The villager depends on caste-based protections and still faces discrimination, so caste is highly visible.

topics.title: Tribe: concept and classification by permanent traits

learn.hook: From the Gonds of central India, numbering in millions, to Andaman island communities of just a few hundred people, 'tribe' covers an astonishing range of communities.
points: 'Tribe' is a modern term, used by colonial and later administrators for communities seen as outside the caste-Hindu fold: no caste, no written-text religion, no state of the usual kind and no sharp class divisions.
Permanent traits used to classify tribes: region, language, physical (racial) characteristics and ecological habitat.
Region: about 85 per cent of the tribal population lives in 'middle India' (from Gujarat and Rajasthan to West Bengal and Odisha); over 11 per cent lives in the North-East.

Language: four families, Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austric and Tibeto-Burman. Austric is spoken entirely by tribal people, and over 80 per cent of Tibeto-Burman speakers are tribal. Physical-racial categories once used: Negrito, Australoid, Mongoloid, Dravidian and Aryan.

Size: tribes range from over a million (Gonds, Bhils, Santhals, Oraons, Minas, Bodos, Mundas) to very small groups such as the Andamanese islanders. Tribal people make up about 8 per cent of India's population.

example.q: Which permanent trait is used when tribes are grouped as 'Austric' or 'Tibeto-Burman'?
steps: Austric and Tibeto-Burman are names of language families.
Language is one of the permanent traits.
So the classification is by language.
example.answer: Language.

learn.reallife: The Santhali language, written in Ol Chiki script, is included in the Eighth Schedule, a recognition of a large Austric-speaking tribal community.

quiz.explain: Tribes were defined in contrast to caste-Hindu society.

quiz.explain: Region, language, physical traits and habitat are permanent traits.

quiz.explain: These were the racial categories; the other lists are languages, livelihoods and varnas.

quiz.explain: Both statements are true, but the national tribal share does not explain why particular tribes are large.
quiz.mistake: Treats any two true, related statements as cause and effect

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do sociologists classify tribes? By where they live? What they speak?'
teach.praise: Region, language, physical traits and habitat: the permanent traits! And most tribal people live in middle India. Tweet!
teach.nudge: But what are the permanent traits, and which language families do tribes speak?

topics.title: Acquired traits and the debate over 'tribe'

learn.hook: Textbooks once pictured tribes as isolated forest dwellers frozen in time. But Gond kings ruled kingdoms, and tribal chiefs traded and fought alongside states for centuries. The real history is very different.
points: Acquired traits used to classify tribes: (1) mode of livelihood: fishers, food gatherers and hunters, shifting cultivators, peasants, and plantation and industrial workers; (2) extent of incorporation into Hindu society.
Debate: many scholars argue tribes were never isolated or 'primitive'. Many were 'secondary' formations, shaped through long contact with states and civilisations.
Historical evidence: Gond kingdoms of central India (such as Garha Mandla and Chanda); tribal chiefdoms; trading links; tribes serving as soldiers and allies of states.

1940s debate on policy: 'isolationists' or protectionists (associated with Verrier Elwin) wanted tribes protected from traders, moneylenders and missionaries; 'integrationists' (associated with G.S. Ghurye, who saw tribes as 'backward Hindus') wanted them integrated into the mainstream.

example.q: A tribe once practised shifting cultivation; now many members work in a steel plant. Which classification captures this change?
steps: Shifting cultivation and industrial work are modes of livelihood.
Livelihood is an acquired trait, so it can change.
The tribe moves from one livelihood category to another.
example.answer: Classification by mode of livelihood, an acquired trait.

learn.reallife: The Gond kingdom of Garha Mandla in present-day Madhya Pradesh, with its forts and queens such as Rani Durgavati, shows that tribal communities built states of their own.

quiz.explain: Trade, military roles and kingdoms prove long contact.

quiz.explain: Incorporation can change over time, so it is acquired.

teach.ask: Gappu peeps out of a tree: 'Weren't tribes always living alone in the forests, cut off from everyone?'
teach.praise: Oh! Tribes traded, fought and even built kingdoms. And scholars argued whether to protect or integrate them. Not isolated at all!
teach.nudge: But what evidence shows tribes were not isolated, and what was the isolation-integration debate?

learn.hook: The big dams and steel plants that powered India's growth were often built on tribal land. For those who lost their homes, 'national development' felt very different.
points: After independence, national development, through large dams, mines, industries and forest policies, often came at the cost of tribal communities, who lost land and forests and were displaced.
Tribal identity today is shaped by forced incorporation into the mainstream and by resistance and assertion against it.
Long movements won statehood for Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh in 2000, but problems of displacement and control over resources continue.
In the North-East, special laws (such as the Armed Forces Special Powers Act) limiting civil liberties have been linked to cycles of rebellion and repression.

Reservations have produced an educated tribal middle class that shapes tribal identity and assertion. Two key issues drive tribal movements: control over vital resources (land, forests) and ethnic-cultural identity.

example.q: A dam floods forest villages of an adivasi community. Which two issues of tribal movements does this raise?
steps: Loss of land and forest is about control over resources.
Loss of sacred sites, language and community life threatens ethnic-cultural identity.
Both issues are combined in the protest.
example.answer: Control over land and forests, and protection of cultural identity.

learn.reallife: Jharkhand, formed in 2000, holds vast mineral wealth; debates over who benefits from its mines show that statehood did not end resource struggles.

teach.praise: So 'national' development often cost tribes their land and forests, and their movements fight for resources and identity. Now I get it.
teach.nudge: But what do tribal movements demand, and what did statehood achieve or fail to achieve?

learn.hook: Think of your own family: who lives with whom, whose surname you carry, who decides big things. Each answer points to a different way of classifying families.
points: Nuclear family: one couple and their unmarried children. Extended (joint) family: more than one couple, often more than two generations, living together.
It is a myth that India had only joint families: nuclear families have always existed, especially among some groups, and joint families were often an ideal of landed upper castes.

By residence: matrilocal (couple lives with the wife's parents) or patrilocal (with the husband's parents). By inheritance/succession: matrilineal (through the mother) or patrilineal (through the father). By authority: matriarchal (women dominant) or patriarchal (men dominant).
Families change accidentally (war, migration, illness) or through deliberate choices. In many urban families grandparents now move in to help with child care while both parents work.
Marriage is changing too: more love marriages and a higher age at marriage, though inter-caste marriages still face resistance.

example.q: Priya, after marriage, lives with her husband in his parents' house; property passes from father to son; the eldest man makes major decisions. Classify this family.
steps: Living with the husband's parents: patrilocal.
Property from father to son: patrilineal.
Men hold authority: patriarchal.
example.answer: Patrilocal, patrilineal and patriarchal.

learn.reallife: Many IT professionals in Bengaluru or Pune live in nuclear flats but bring parents from their home towns to help raise children, a new shape of the 'joint' family.

teach.nudge: But how do we classify families by residence, inheritance and authority?

topics.title: Matriliny, matriarchy and gender: the Khasi example

learn.hook: Among the Khasis of Meghalaya, property passes from mother to daughter. Does that make it a society ruled by women? The answer is a lesson in reading sociological terms carefully.
points: Matrilineal societies in India include the Khasis of Meghalaya and the Nairs of Kerala.
Among the Khasis, property passes from mother to daughter, but control over it rests with the mother's brother (maternal uncle).
This creates role strain for men: they are torn between responsibilities to their natal family (sister's household) and to their wife and children.
Matriliny is not matriarchy: inheritance through women does not mean women hold power. Matriarchy remains a theoretical concept with no clear historical or ethnographic example.
In most Indian families, patriarchal norms and son preference shape decisions on inheritance, education and even survival of girls.

example.q: Explain why a Khasi woman who inherits ancestral property may still not control it.
steps: Khasi descent and inheritance run through women: matriliny.
But managing and controlling property is the job of her brother or maternal uncle.
So ownership by inheritance and authority are separated, and men keep authority.
example.answer: Matriliny gives women inheritance, but authority stays with men, so it is not matriarchy.

learn.reallife: Meghalaya's matrilineal customs often surprise visitors, yet debates there about men's rights and women's role in traditional councils show that inheritance and power are different things.

teach.nudge: But who controls property in Khasi society, and how is matriliny different from matriarchy?

chapters.title: Indian Society: Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion

learn.hook: A sweeper and a bank manager may both start work at 9 a.m. One woke at 4 to fetch water and catch two buses; the other was driven to office. Is the difference just about talent?
points: Institutions such as caste, tribe, family and the market do not only organise society; they also produce inequality and exclusion.
Inequality often looks natural or deserved, as if the poor are poor because of their own failings. This leads people to 'blame the victim'.
Sociology shows that most inequality is group-based: people's chances depend on the caste, class, gender, region or community they are born into, not only on individual talent, effort or luck.
A useful activity: compare a typical day of people at different levels (a domestic worker, a clerk, a business owner) by interviewing them. The patterns reveal structured inequality.

example.q: Two students score differently in Class 12. One had a private tutor, a quiet room and a laptop; the other worked in a shop after school. What would a sociologist say?
steps: Individual effort matters, but resources differed sharply.
These resources came from family class position, not from the students themselves.
Such differences repeat across groups, so they are social, not just individual.
example.answer: The gap is shaped largely by group-based, social inequality in resources.

learn.reallife: Surveys of NEET and JEE toppers often show many come from families who could afford coaching in Kota or Hyderabad, a reminder that 'merit' grows on social soil.

games.title: Natural or social?
items: Inequality between groups usually reflects only differences in individual talent.
Group-based differences, not just talent, explain most inequality.
Institutions like caste and the market can produce inequality.
They distribute resources unequally.
Blaming the poor for their poverty ignores social causes.
Sociology looks at structured disadvantage.
Interviewing people of different job levels can reveal patterns of inequality.
This is a suggested activity in the chapter.
If inequality seems natural, it must be natural.
Inequality often only appears natural.

games.title: Individual or social explanation?
