Women earn less than men for similar work
He was born more talented
Dalit households own less land on average

quiz.q: According to the chapter, social institutions such as caste and the market:
options: Ensure perfect equality for everyone
Have no link with inequality at all
Exist only in rural areas of India
Also produce inequality and exclusion
quiz.explain: These institutions distribute resources and opportunities unequally.

quiz.q: Why do many people believe inequality is natural?
options: It often appears to be deserved or inborn
Census data prove it is natural
Sociologists have shown it is natural
Laws describe it as natural
quiz.explain: Inequality can look natural, which leads to blaming the poor.

quiz.q: 'Blaming the victim' means:
options: Punishing criminals for the offences they commit
Holding the poor responsible for their own poverty
Blaming the rich for all of society's problems
Recording the names of victims in police reports
quiz.explain: It ignores the social causes of disadvantage.

quiz.q: Sociology explains most social inequality in terms of:
options: Purely individual talent or effort and nothing else
Group-based differences in resources and opportunity
Pure chance and luck that nobody can control
Natural factors such as the weather and climate
quiz.explain: Group membership shapes life chances.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Inequality is often social rather than individual.
Reason (R): People's chances are shaped by the groups they are born into.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Birth into caste, class or gender groups shapes opportunities.
quiz.mistake: Misses the group basis of inequality

quiz.q: Which observation best shows that an inequality is social?
options: It repeats across a whole group over time
It affects one unlucky person once
It is caused by a single accident
It disappears when a person tries harder
quiz.explain: Patterns across groups and generations reveal social inequality.
quiz.mistake: Treats one-off cases as social patterns

quiz.q: A student interviews a domestic worker and a bank officer about their daily routines. This activity helps to:
options: Prove that everyone has exactly the same day
Reveal structured inequality in everyday life
Measure the crude birth rate of a town
Test the theory of demographic transition
quiz.explain: Comparing routines shows how class shapes daily life.
quiz.mistake: Misreads the purpose of the activity

quiz.q: Which statement would a sociologist most likely reject?
options: Group membership shapes people's life chances
Institutions such as caste can produce exclusion
The poor are poor only because they do not work hard
Inequality can look natural without being natural
quiz.explain: This statement blames the victim and ignores social causes.
quiz.mistake: Agrees with the 'blame the poor' view

teach.ask: Gappu says: 'Isn't it simple? People who work hard succeed; those who don't, stay poor.'
teach.praise: Oops, I was blaming the victim! Inequality mostly comes from the groups we're born into and how institutions work.
teach.nudge: But is it only about individual effort? What role do groups and institutions play?

topics.title: Social inequality and Bourdieu's three capitals

learn.hook: A doctor's daughter inherits not just money but books at home, polished English and contacts who can recommend her for internships. Pierre Bourdieu called these different kinds of capital.
points: Inequality is social in three senses: it is about groups, not just individuals; it is not only economic (it includes status, education and power); and it is systematic and structured.
Social inequality is the unequal distribution of socially valued resources: money, property, education, health, power and prestige.

Pierre Bourdieu identified three forms of capital: economic capital (material assets and income), cultural capital (educational qualifications and status) and social capital (networks of contacts and social associations).
These forms can be converted into one another: money can buy good education (economic → cultural), education can get a good job (cultural → economic), and contacts can open doors (social → economic).

example.q: Classify: (a) a flat in Mumbai, (b) an IIT degree, (c) an uncle who is a senior officer and recommends you.
steps: (a) Material asset: economic capital.
(b) Educational qualification: cultural capital.
(c) Network and contacts: social capital.
example.answer: (a) economic, (b) cultural, (c) social capital.

learn.reallife: LinkedIn connections, alumni networks of top colleges and family business contacts are modern forms of social capital that help some people get jobs faster.

games.title: Which form of capital?
items: Land and shares
Bank savings
A university degree
Fluent English and refined tastes
Family contacts in government
Membership of an elite club

quiz.q: Who identified economic, cultural and social capital?
options: Pierre Bourdieu
Karl Marx
Emile Durkheim
M.N. Srinivas
quiz.explain: Bourdieu developed the three forms of capital.

quiz.q: Educational qualifications are an example of:
options: Economic capital
Cultural capital
Social capital
Physical capital
quiz.explain: Bourdieu classes education and status as cultural capital.

quiz.q: Networks of contacts and associations are:
options: Social capital
Economic capital
Cultural capital
Ritual capital
quiz.explain: Social capital refers to useful relationships.

quiz.q: A wealthy family pays for its son's education at a top college. This shows:
options: Conversion of social into economic capital
Conversion of economic into cultural capital
Conversion of cultural into social capital
No conversion between capitals
quiz.explain: Money (economic) buys education (cultural).

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three senses in which inequality is social?
options: It depends only on individual talent
It is about groups, not just individuals
It is not only economic
It is systematic and structured
quiz.explain: Social inequality goes beyond individual differences.
quiz.mistake: Picks a true feature as false

quiz.q: Social inequality is best defined as the unequal distribution of:
options: Rainfall and sunshine across different regions
Socially valued resources like money, education and power
Natural height and weight among different people
Holidays and working days across the months of a year
quiz.explain: It is about valued social resources.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Children of well-connected families often find jobs more easily.
Reason (R): Social capital can be converted into economic advantage.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Contacts (social capital) open doors to jobs (economic capital).

quiz.q: How is social inequality different from individual inequality?
options: It is patterned by group membership and structured
It concerns only one person's unique abilities
It is always caused by luck and nothing else
It is never linked to resources or opportunity
quiz.explain: Social inequality follows group lines systematically.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Isn't capital just money? What is Bourdieu talking about with three capitals?'
teach.praise: Wow, money, education and contacts are all capital, and they can turn into each other. Bourdieu is one smart bird!
teach.nudge: But what are the three forms of capital, and how can one become another?

learn.hook: If your grandparents were landless labourers, what are the odds that you will own a business? Social stratification is the reason the answer is not '50-50'.
points: Social stratification is a society-wide system that ranks categories of people in a hierarchy. Your place in it shapes your life chances: education, health, income, even life expectancy.
Principle 1: stratification is a characteristic of society, not simply a function of individual differences. It becomes elaborate as societies produce surplus wealth to be distributed.
Principle 2: stratification persists over generations. It is closely linked to the family and inheritance of resources; ascribed status (such as caste) and endogamy keep it going.
Principle 3: stratification is supported by patterns of belief or ideology. For example, the caste system was justified by ideas of purity and pollution.

example.q: Which principle of stratification does each show? (a) Children of rich parents inherit property; (b) caste rank was justified by ritual purity; (c) whole categories of people, not just individuals, are ranked.
steps: (a) Inheritance across generations: Principle 2.
(b) Belief justifies inequality: Principle 3.
(c) A feature of society, not of individuals: Principle 1.
example.answer: (a) Principle 2; (b) Principle 3; (c) Principle 1.

learn.reallife: Studies of top company boards in India find many directors from a few communities and families, showing how stratification persists across generations.

games.title: Match the principle
pairs: A feature of society, not individual difference
Opportunities shaped by one's place in the hierarchy

games.title: Stratification check
items: Stratification is only about individual differences in ability.
It is a feature of society.
Inheritance and endogamy help stratification persist over generations.
Families pass on status and resources.
Ideas of purity and pollution supported the caste hierarchy.
Ideology legitimises stratification.
Stratification has no effect on a person's life chances.
Position shapes education, health and income.
Stratification becomes more elaborate as societies produce surplus wealth.
Surplus creates unequal shares to distribute.

quiz.q: Social stratification refers to:
options: Layers of rock formed deep inside the earth
Differences in the personal tastes of individuals
A system ranking categories of people in a hierarchy
An official list of government departments
quiz.explain: It is the structured ranking of groups.

quiz.q: 'Stratification is a characteristic of society' means that:
options: Every person freely chooses their own social rank
It exists only in a few unusual and isolated families
It depends entirely on luck and pure chance alone
It is not simply a result of individual differences
quiz.explain: Stratification is built into society's structure.

quiz.q: Which practice helps stratification persist over generations?
options: Equal schooling for all children
Random allocation of jobs by lottery
Inheritance of property and endogamy
Free and frequent inter-caste marriage
quiz.explain: Passing on resources within closed groups maintains inequality.

quiz.q: The idea that caste rank depends on purity and pollution illustrates which principle?
options: Stratification is supported by belief
Stratification persists over generations
Stratification depends on talent
Stratification is temporary
quiz.explain: Ideology justifies and supports inequality.

quiz.q: 'Life chances' in sociology refers to:
options: Opportunities in health, education and income
The chance of winning a state-run lottery
A person's fortune as told by an astrologer
A team's chances of winning a cricket match
quiz.explain: Life chances depend on one's place in the stratification system.

quiz.q: Ascribed status is:
options: Status earned through hard effort
Status won in an open election
Status bought with money or gifts
Status given at birth, such as caste
quiz.explain: Ascription is by birth; achievement is by effort.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Stratification tends to persist over generations.
Reason (R): Families pass on resources and status to their children.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Inheritance and family transmission keep stratification going.

quiz.q: Why does stratification become more elaborate as societies develop surplus?
options: Surplus removes every kind of inequality between people
Surplus makes every member of society equally rich
Surplus brings the inheritance of property to an end
Surplus creates wealth that can be shared unequally
quiz.explain: With surplus comes unequal control over it.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is social stratification, and why do the same families stay on top for ages?'
teach.praise: So stratification is society's ladder, passed down through families and justified by beliefs. Three principles, one sharp bird!
teach.nudge: But what are the three principles of social stratification?

learn.hook: In many old films, a character from one community is always the comic servant, another always the villain. These portrayals are not harmless fun; they shape how real people are treated.
points: Prejudice: pre-formed opinions or attitudes held by members of one group about another, based on hearsay rather than evidence, and resistant to change even when new information appears. Prejudice can be negative or positive.

Stereotypes: fixed and inflexible images of a group, applied to all its members while ignoring individual variation. Example: the colonial idea of 'martial races', which labelled some communities as naturally warlike.

Discrimination: actual behaviour or practice that disqualifies members of a group from opportunities (jobs, housing, education). It may be open or hidden, and is often justified with other reasons such as 'merit'.
Prejudice is an attitude; discrimination is action. Prejudice can exist without discrimination, and discrimination can occur without open prejudice.
Activity: analyse how films or novels portray groups, and notice prejudiced or stereotyped portrayals.

example.q: A landlord believes people of a certain community are 'unclean' (A) and refuses to rent his flat to a family from that community (B). Identify A and B.
steps: A is an opinion not based on evidence and applied to a whole group: prejudice (resting on a stereotype).
B is actual behaviour denying an opportunity: discrimination.
example.answer: A: prejudice; B: discrimination.

learn.reallife: Housing advertisements that say 'only vegetarians' or 'family only' have been questioned for hiding discrimination behind apparently neutral rules.

games.title: Attitude or action?
items: Believing a group is lazy
Refusing a job interview to that group
Assuming all members of a community are good at business
Denying a flat on rent because of caste
Disliking a group without knowing any member
Paying women less for the same work

games.title: Match the term
pairs: Pre-judged opinion not based on evidence

quiz.q: Prejudice refers to:
options: Pre-formed opinions about a group, not based on evidence
Behaviour that actually denies jobs to a whole group
A legal judgement delivered in a court case
A conclusion reached only after careful research
quiz.explain: Prejudice is an attitude formed in advance of evidence.

quiz.q: Prejudice can be:
options: Only negative, never positive
Only positive, never negative
Either positive or negative
Neither positive nor negative
quiz.explain: Prejudice may favour or disfavour a group; both are pre-judgements.

quiz.q: The colonial idea of 'martial races' is an example of:
options: A stereotype
Social capital
Endogamy
Demographic dividend
quiz.explain: It assigned a fixed trait to entire communities.

quiz.q: Discrimination is best described as:
options: An opinion held only in one's own mind
Behaviour that denies a group opportunities
A fixed mental image held about a group
A natural, inborn difference between people
quiz.explain: Discrimination is action, not just attitude.

quiz.q: Why is discrimination often hard to prove?
options: It may be hidden behind reasons such as 'merit'
It is always openly announced by employers
It is perfectly legal everywhere in India
It happens only in films, not in real life
quiz.explain: Discriminators rarely state the real reason.

quiz.q: A stereotype ignores:
options: The name by which the group is known
The very existence of the group
The language spoken by the group
Variation among individuals in the group
quiz.explain: Stereotypes apply a single image to everyone.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Prejudice is resistant to change.
Reason (R): Prejudiced views are often retained even when new evidence contradicts them.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Resistance to evidence is exactly what makes prejudice persist.

quiz.q: A student studies how a community is shown in popular films. She is mainly examining:
options: Birth and death rates in the region
Land ceiling laws in different states
Wages paid in film industry jobs
Prejudiced and stereotyped portrayals
quiz.explain: Media portrayals can carry and spread stereotypes.
quiz.mistake: Misses the purpose of the activity

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Aren't prejudice and discrimination the same thing?'
teach.praise: Prejudice is a pre-judged attitude, a stereotype is a fixed image, and discrimination is the action. Three different birds!
teach.nudge: But which one is an attitude and which one is an action? And what is a stereotype?

topics.title: Social exclusion and the limits of law

learn.hook: Imagine a village where one community cannot draw water from the main well, a bank branch that ignores a woman without proper papers, and a hospital that treats a transgender patient with contempt. All are forms of social exclusion.
points: Social exclusion: the ways in which individuals or groups are cut off from full participation in the wider society, including access to services such as health, education, banking, transport and police protection.
Exclusion is involuntary and structural: it is practised regardless of the wishes of those excluded. It is not about individuals choosing to stay away.
Prolonged exclusion can lead the excluded to stop trying to participate, which can then be wrongly read as their own 'choice'.
Law alone cannot end prejudice and exclusion. Sustained campaigns to change social attitudes and practices are needed alongside legal protections.

Transgender and third-gender people have faced deep exclusion. The Supreme Court recognised the 'third gender' in 2014 (NALSA judgment), and the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was passed in 2019.

example.q: A Dalit family stops sending its children to a village school after years of humiliation there. Some say, 'They don't value education.' What would a sociologist say?
steps: The family was excluded through humiliation: involuntary and structural.
Repeated exclusion led them to stop trying.
Calling it their 'choice' hides the exclusion behind it.
example.answer: It is the result of exclusion, not a voluntary choice.

learn.reallife: Jan Dhan accounts were opened for crores of people who had never had a bank account, an attempt to reduce one form of exclusion, from the banking system.

games.title: Exclusion check
items: Social exclusion is something people usually choose for themselves.
It is involuntary and structural.
Exclusion can include denial of access to banks, hospitals and police.
It covers full participation in society's services.
Laws alone are enough to end prejudice.
Social campaigns are also needed.
The Supreme Court recognised a 'third gender' in 2014.
This was the NALSA judgment.
Long-term exclusion can make people stop trying to participate.
This can then be misread as choice.

options: involuntary
voluntary
temporary

items.text: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was passed in ___.
Law alone cannot end prejudice; sustained social ___ are needed.
options: campaigns
censuses
markets

quiz.q: Social exclusion means:
options: Being cut off from full participation in society
Choosing to live alone in the hills by choice
Being selected by society for a special honour
Moving to another country for higher studies
quiz.explain: It is about denial of participation and access.

quiz.q: Social exclusion is described as involuntary because:
options: People happily choose it for themselves
It happens regardless of the wishes of the excluded
It is always temporary and soon comes to an end
It affects only the rich and powerful groups
quiz.explain: The excluded do not choose their exclusion.

quiz.q: Which is an example of social exclusion?
options: A student choosing to skip a classmate's party
A family moving to another town for a new job
A person preferring tea to coffee in the morning
A group denied access to a public water source
quiz.explain: Denial of access to common services is exclusion.

quiz.q: Why might excluded groups stop trying to take part in society?
options: They have everything they need
The law forbids them to participate
They are paid to stay away
Repeated rejection discourages them
quiz.explain: Long exclusion produces withdrawal, which is misread as choice.

quiz.q: The 2014 NALSA judgment of the Supreme Court is linked to:
options: Abolition of untouchability in law
Reservation for OBCs in central jobs
The Right to Information for citizens
Legal recognition of the third gender
quiz.explain: It recognised transgender persons as a third gender.
quiz.mistake: Mixes it up with other legal milestones

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Laws against discrimination are necessary but not sufficient.
Reason (R): Prejudice is rooted in social attitudes that law alone cannot change.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: Changing attitudes needs social effort beyond law.

quiz.q: Which statement about social exclusion is correct?
options: It is always a personal choice
It affects only individuals, not groups
It is the same as poverty
It is structural, not just individual
quiz.explain: Exclusion is built into social structures.

quiz.q: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was passed in:
quiz.explain: The Act came in 2019, after the 2014 NALSA judgment.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the Act with the judgment year

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If some people don't use the village well or the bank, isn't that just their choice?'
teach.praise: So exclusion is forced on people by society, not chosen, and fixing it needs both laws and changed attitudes.
teach.nudge: But is exclusion really a choice? What makes it involuntary and structural?

learn.hook: Look at any national survey of poverty by social group and the ranking barely changes: Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Castes at the bottom, upper castes at the top. Caste and class still march together.
points: Caste is a system that legitimises discrimination; it can be humiliating, exclusionary and exploitative for those at the bottom.

In the ideal model, ritual status (purity) and economic status were supposed to be separate. In practice, caste and class overlapped strongly: upper castes held land and power; lower castes were mostly poor.
Since the 19th century the link between caste and occupation has weakened, but at the macro level the caste-class correlation remains strong.

Poverty data (e.g. 2011-12) show the pattern: Scheduled Tribes have the highest proportion of poor people, followed by Scheduled Castes, then OBCs, while upper castes have the lowest poverty and the largest share of the affluent, in both rural and urban areas.

A comparison: apartheid in South Africa was a legal system of racial segregation, fought by the African National Congress and Nelson Mandela; it ended in 1994 with the first democratic elections. Race there, like caste here, tied identity to inequality.

example.q: A table shows poverty in 2011-12: ST highest, then SC, then OBC, then upper castes lowest. What conclusion can be drawn?
steps: The ranking of poverty closely follows the caste hierarchy.
This holds in both rural and urban areas.
So caste and economic status still correlate strongly.
example.answer: Caste and class remain strongly linked at the macro level.

learn.reallife: Nelson Mandela, imprisoned for 27 years, became South Africa's first black president in 1994; Indians often compare the anti-apartheid struggle with the struggle against caste discrimination.

quiz.explain: In theory ritual purity was distinct from wealth; in practice they overlapped.

quiz.explain: Occupations have opened up, but group-level inequality persists.

quiz.explain: Apartheid enforced racial separation by law until 1994.

quiz.explain: The ANC, with Nelson Mandela, led the struggle.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Caste continues to matter for economic inequality.
Reason (R): Poverty rates still follow the caste hierarchy at the group level.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Group-level poverty data show the continuing link.
quiz.mistake: Thinks caste has no economic effect today

quiz.q: Caste is described as a discriminatory system because it is:
options: Humiliating, exclusionary and exploitative
Voluntary, flexible and equal for all
Based only on individual merit and effort
Limited only to religious rituals at home
quiz.explain: These three aspects describe how caste harms those at the bottom.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Doesn't caste only matter for rituals now? What has it got to do with who is rich or poor?'
teach.praise: Wow, poverty still follows the caste ladder: ST and SC at the bottom, upper castes at the top. Caste is about class too!
teach.nudge: But how do caste and class relate today? What do the poverty figures show?

learn.hook: In some places, Dalits were once forbidden from even letting their shadow fall on an upper-caste person. Untouchability is the most extreme form of caste discrimination.
points: Untouchability is an extreme and especially vicious aspect of the caste system that prescribes stringent social sanctions against members of castes located at the bottom of the purity-pollution scale, who are considered polluting.
It is found across India, though its forms and intensity vary by region.

Three dimensions: exclusion (denied access to water sources, temples, ceremonies), humiliation-subordination (forced gestures of deference, such as removing footwear), and exploitation (forced, unpaid or underpaid labour).
In parts of southern India, 'distance pollution' meant that even the presence or shadow of a so-called untouchable was considered polluting.

Names: Gandhi used 'Harijan' (children of God). The groups themselves chose 'Dalit' (meaning oppressed or downtrodden), popularised by the Dalit Panthers in the 1970s. 'Dalit' asserts identity, not pity.

example.q: Classify each practice by the dimension of untouchability: (a) not allowed to enter a temple; (b) forced to remove footwear before upper castes; (c) made to do unpaid labour at village functions.
steps: (a) Denial of access: exclusion.
(b) Forced deference: humiliation-subordination.
(c) Unpaid labour: exploitation.
example.answer: (a) exclusion; (b) humiliation-subordination; (c) exploitation.

learn.reallife: Dalit literature and autobiographies, now taught in universities and translated widely, use the word 'Dalit' with pride, as a symbol of resistance.

games.title: Which dimension?

quiz.explain: This form was found in parts of southern India.

options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false

quiz.explain: Self-naming expresses dignity and assertion rather than pity.
quiz.mistake: Misses why the term is preferred

teach.ask: Gappu whispers: 'What exactly is untouchability, and why do people say Dalit instead of Harijan?'
teach.praise: Untouchability has three faces: exclusion, humiliation and exploitation. And 'Dalit' is a proud, self-chosen name. I'll use it right!
teach.nudge: But what are the three dimensions of untouchability, and what does 'Dalit' mean?

topics.title: Fighting caste discrimination: state and non-state efforts

learn.hook: From a law of 1850 to the Constitution's Article 17 and the Atrocities Act of 1989, Indian law has slowly built a wall against caste discrimination. Dalit movements built the pressure that made those laws happen.
points: State initiatives: Scheduled lists of castes and tribes from 1935; reservation of seats in legislatures, government jobs and educational institutions for SCs and STs.

Key laws: Caste Disabilities Removal Act, 1850 (citizens' rights not to be curtailed due to change of religion or caste); Article 17 of the Constitution abolishing untouchability; SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989; 93rd Amendment (2005) enabling OBC reservation in higher education.
Non-state initiatives: Dalit movements and leaders such as Jyotiba Phule, Periyar (E.V. Ramaswamy), Iyothee Thass and B.R. Ambedkar fought for dignity and equality.

Dalit political parties, Dalit literature in Marathi, Kannada, Tamil, Hindi and other languages, and poems such as Daya Pawar's 'The City', which shows caste surviving beneath a modern urban surface, are forms of assertion.
Activity: list the constitutional articles and laws relating to SCs, STs and untouchability.

example.q: Arrange these legal milestones in order: Atrocities Act; Article 17 in the Constitution; Caste Disabilities Removal Act; 93rd Amendment.
steps: Caste Disabilities Removal Act: 1850.
Article 17: Constitution in force from 1950.
SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act: 1989.
93rd Amendment: 2005.

learn.reallife: Reserved constituencies in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies, and SC/ST quotas in central universities and the UPSC, are everyday reminders of state initiatives against caste inequality.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What has India done to fight caste discrimination? Is it only the government?'
teach.praise: So the state gave Article 17, reservations and the Atrocities Act, while Dalit movements and literature pushed from below. Teamwork!
teach.nudge: But what laws and policies exist, and what did non-state movements contribute?

learn.hook: In 1990, the decision to implement the Mandal Commission report set off fierce debates across India's campuses. Who are the Other Backward Classes, and why did their inclusion matter so much?
points: OBCs are castes of low ritual status, above the 'untouchable' groups but below the upper castes; many are service and artisan castes. They were not subjected to untouchability, which distinguishes them from Dalits.
The Constitution uses the idea of 'socially and educationally backward classes'. OBCs exist among non-Hindu religions too, for example among Muslims and Christians.
The First Backward Classes Commission was headed by Kaka Kalelkar (1953). The Second, the B.P. Mandal Commission, reported in 1980; its recommendations were implemented in 1990.
Southern states had backward class movements and reservation policies much earlier, in the first half of the 20th century.
OBCs are internally divided: landed, dominant upper OBCs (often powerful in rural areas) versus poor lower OBCs, mainly artisans and service castes.

example.q: How are OBCs different from Dalits?
steps: Dalits faced untouchability, the most extreme form of exclusion.
OBCs had low ritual status but were not 'untouchable'.
OBCs include both landed dominant castes and poor service castes; they also exist among non-Hindus.
example.answer: OBCs are low-status but not untouchable, and are internally more varied.

learn.reallife: The 27 per cent OBC reservation in central government jobs and central educational institutions traces back to the Mandal Commission and the 93rd Amendment.

learn.hook: In the forests of central India, families who had gathered mahua and tendu leaves for generations suddenly became 'encroachers' on land declared to be state forest. Adivasi struggles begin with such stories.
points: Scheduled Tribes face poverty, powerlessness and social stigma, similar in some ways to Dalits but with different roots.
Colonial forest policy declared forests state property, turned adivasis into 'encroachers' on their own lands, and restricted shifting cultivation and gathering of forest produce.

After independence, mines, dams and industries displaced huge numbers of adivasis, often without fair compensation or rehabilitation, e.g. the Sardar Sarovar dam on the Narmada and the Polavaram project on the Godavari.
Liberalisation after 1991 made it easier for corporations to acquire land in tribal areas.

'Adivasi' (original inhabitants) is a political term of assertion; 'diku' means outsiders (traders, moneylenders, officials). Adivasis lived in contiguous areas, unlike Dalits, which helped movements win the states of Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh (2000).

example.q: Why could adivasis win separate states while Dalits could not demand a state of their own?
steps: Adivasis were concentrated in contiguous regions, such as the Chota Nagpur plateau.
Dalits are spread across villages all over India, not in one block of territory.
Territorial concentration made statehood a realistic demand for adivasis.
example.answer: Contiguous territorial concentration of adivasis made statehood possible.

learn.reallife: Protests over the Sardar Sarovar dam, led by the Narmada Bachao Andolan, drew national attention to the displacement of adivasi villages in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat.

teach.nudge: But what happened to adivasi land and forests, and what did their struggles achieve?

learn.hook: In 1905, Begum Rokeya imagined a 'Ladyland' where women ran the country and men stayed indoors. It was one of the earliest science fiction stories by an Indian woman, and a sharp critique of purdah.
points: Gender inequality is social, not natural. Evidence: matrilineal societies like the Nairs and Khasis, and women who were major farmers and traders in parts of Africa, show women's roles vary by society.

The 'women's question' arose in 19th-century middle-class reform movements. Raja Rammohun Roy (Brahmo Samaj) campaigned against sati; M.G. Ranade argued for widow remarriage using both scriptures and Western moral philosophy.

Jyotiba Phule (Satyashodhak Samaj) attacked caste and gender oppression together. Sir Syed Ahmed Khan sought reform within Islam and favoured girls' education at home; Dayanand Saraswati took a broadly similar approach to women's education.
Tarabai Shinde's 'Stree Purush Tulana' (1882) protested the double standards of a male-dominated society.
Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain's 'Sultana's Dream' (1905) is a role-reversed utopia, an early work of science fiction in English by an Indian woman.

example.q: Match each reformer to a contribution: Rammohun Roy, Tarabai Shinde, Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain.
steps: Rammohun Roy: campaigned against sati (Brahmo Samaj).
Tarabai Shinde: 'Stree Purush Tulana' (1882) against double standards.
Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain: 'Sultana's Dream' (1905), a role-reversed utopia.
example.answer: Roy: anti-sati; Shinde: Stree Purush Tulana; Rokeya: Sultana's Dream.

learn.reallife: Phule and his wife Savitribai opened schools for girls in Pune; today Savitribai Phule Pune University is named after her.

teach.praise: So gender inequality is social, and reformers like Roy, Ranade, Phule, Tarabai Shinde and Rokeya challenged it in the 19th century!
teach.nudge: But which reformers raised women's issues, and how do we know gender inequality is social?

topics.title: Women's movement in the 20th century and beyond

learn.hook: In 1931, decades before independence, the Indian National Congress at Karachi promised women equal rights as citizens. Turning that promise into reality took a whole movement.
points: Early 20th century: women's organisations were formed at national and local levels, and many women took part in the national movement.
The Karachi Session of the Indian National Congress (1931) adopted a resolution on Fundamental Rights and economic policy that committed to women's equality as citizens.
After a lull, the women's movement revived in the 1970s, and in the 1980s campaigns for legal reform took up issues like rape, dowry deaths and violence against women.
New challenges include the declining child sex ratio and sex-selective abortion.
Activities: study a local reformer; list jobs open and closed to women; group projects on women's reservation or domestic violence.

example.q: List three issues the women's movement has taken up over time.
steps: Early phase: education, sati, widow remarriage, participation in the national movement.
1970s-80s: rape laws, dowry deaths, violence against women.
Recent: the declining child sex ratio.
example.answer: Reform of social customs, legal reform against violence, and the sex ratio.

learn.reallife: Many panchayats now have women sarpanches because of one-third reservation for women in local bodies, an outcome of long campaigns.

learn.hook: In the film 'Iqbal', a boy who cannot hear or speak dreams of bowling for India. His biggest hurdle is not his body, but people who refuse to give him a chance.
points: Disability is social, not only biological: society is built in ways that exclude people with impairments (steps without ramps, no sign language, inaccessible schools and courts).

Anita Ghai notes that disabled people are often invisible in society. Common perceptions treat disability as biological, see the disabled as victims and dependents, and assume disability shapes their self-perception.

Derogatory terms and the 'bechara' (pitiable) attitude reflect cultural beliefs that impairment is fate or the result of karma, seen in myths and folklore. Newer terms such as 'differently abled' and 'visually impaired' reject insulting labels.
Poverty and disability reinforce each other: malnutrition and poor health care cause impairments, and disability reduces earning chances.
The Census 2011 counted disability in eight categories. Laws: the Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995, and later the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, take a rights-based approach.

example.q: A wheelchair user cannot reach a district court on the first floor without a ramp or lift. Is the disability in her body or in the building?
steps: Her impairment is physical.
But the barrier that stops her is the design of the building.
A ramp or lift would remove the barrier.
example.answer: The disabling barrier is social: the building, not just her body.

learn.reallife: Accessible India Campaign (Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan) aims to make public buildings, railway stations and websites accessible, treating disability as a matter of design and rights.

quiz.q:

options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false

quiz.explain: Cultural stories reinforce the belief that disability is fate.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Isn't disability just about the body? Why do sociologists call it social?'
teach.praise: So bodies have impairments, but society's stairs, attitudes and poverty create disability. Let's build ramps, not pity!
teach.nudge: But how does society create disability, and how are poverty and disability linked?

chapters.title: Indian Society: The Challenges of Cultural Diversity

topics.title: Cultural diversity and why it is challenging

learn.hook: When Karnataka and Tamil Nadu argue over Cauvery water, the dispute is about a river, but the passions on the street are about identity. That is why cultural diversity can be both a treasure and a challenge.
points: Cultural diversity means the presence of different types of social and cultural communities: groups defined by language, religion, sect, race or caste. It refers to differences, not inequalities.
Diversity is challenging because cultural identities are very powerful; they can arouse intense passions and mobilise large numbers of people.
Diversity often overlaps with economic and social inequalities, so one community may feel deprived compared with another.
Competition over scarce resources, such as river waters, jobs or government funds, can turn cultural differences into conflict.
India is one of the most culturally diverse nations in the world, with many languages, religions, castes, tribes and regional cultures.

example.q: Why can a dispute over sharing river water between two states turn into an identity conflict?
steps: The water is a scarce resource needed by farmers in both states.
Each state is also a linguistic-cultural community.
Competition over the resource is read as a threat to one's community.
Identity passions then intensify the economic dispute.
example.answer: Scarce resources plus powerful cultural identities can turn differences into conflict.

learn.reallife: A Republic Day parade, with tableaux from every state in different languages, dress and music, celebrates the same diversity that politicians must manage every day.

learn.hook: Nobody chooses their mother tongue, their family's religion or the region they are born in. Yet these unchosen belongings can feel like the core of who we are.
points: Community identity is ascriptive: it is based on birth and belonging, not on any form of achievement or qualification. We belong because we were born into it.
Membership is unconditional; we do not have to earn it, and it is very hard to escape. Even if we disown it, others may continue to identify us by it.
It is formed through socialisation by 'significant others' (parents, family, kin, community). The mother tongue is a key carrier of culture and identity.
Community ties give people security and meaning, so any threat to them provokes strong emotional reactions.
Identity conflicts are hard to resolve because each side sees the other as a mirror image: each feels it is the victim and the other is the aggressor.

example.q: Ravi, born in a Tamil-speaking family, moves to Delhi and rarely speaks Tamil. Why might people still call him 'the Tamil boy'?
steps: His community identity was ascribed at birth.
Membership is unconditional and hard to escape.
Others continue to identify him by it, whatever his own choices.
example.answer: Ascriptive identity persists because others keep recognising it.

learn.reallife: Diaspora associations of Malayalis in the Gulf or Gujaratis in East Africa show how strongly community identity travels with people across borders.

teach.nudge: But how is community identity formed, and why is it so hard to escape?

learn.hook: The Soviet Union was one state with dozens of nationalities. The Jewish and Indian diasporas have members spread across many states. So is a nation the same as a state? Not quite.
points: A nation is a peculiar sort of community: easy to describe but hard to define. It is a large-scale 'community of communities' whose members share a desire to be one political collectivity.
Nations cannot be defined by any single common feature: there are nations without a common language, religion or ethnicity.
State (Max Weber): a body of political-legal institutions that claims control over a particular territory and a monopoly of legitimate force within it.

A nation-state is a nation that has its own state. There is no fixed relationship: one state may contain several nations (the former Soviet Union), and one nation may be spread across many states (diasporas, dual citizenship).
Modern states seek legitimacy by claiming to represent 'the people' and the nation.

example.q: Why is it hard to define a nation by a single feature such as language?
steps: Some nations have many languages (India, Switzerland).
Some nations share a language with others (many Spanish-speaking nations).
So language is neither necessary nor sufficient.
The key is a shared desire to be one political community.
example.answer: No single feature defines a nation; it is a community of communities sharing political aspirations.

learn.reallife: Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) cards for the Indian diaspora show how belonging to a nation can stretch beyond the borders of the Indian state.

teach.nudge: But how is a nation different from a state, and can one exist without the other?

topics.title: Assimilation, integration and the cost of suppression

learn.hook: Some states have tried to make everyone speak one language, celebrate the same holidays and honour the same heroes. History shows this often backfires.
points: Many states are suspicious of cultural diversity, fearing it threatens national unity. They try to suppress or reduce it through assimilation or integration policies.
Assimilation: persuading, encouraging or forcing all citizens to adopt a uniform set of cultural values and norms, usually those of the dominant group.
Integration: insisting that public culture be restricted to a common national pattern, while minority cultures are kept to the private sphere.

Typical homogenising measures: centralising power; one official language imposed everywhere; a single national education system and textbooks; dominant group's history, symbols and holidays as national ones; seizing land and resources of minorities.
Suppressing diversity is costly and often backfires, alienating minorities and provoking conflict. Recognising and accommodating diversity is wiser.

example.q: A country makes the majority language the only language of courts and schools and replaces minority festivals with national holidays. Is this assimilation or integration?
steps: Minorities are being pushed to adopt the dominant culture in all spheres.
Their own culture is not merely kept private; it is being replaced.
This is the definition of assimilation.
example.answer: Assimilation.

learn.reallife: India's Eighth Schedule recognising 22 languages, and courts and exams in many languages, is the opposite of a 'one language' homogenising policy.

teach.praise: Oh no, forcing one culture often backfires! Recognising diversity is the smarter way to unity.
teach.nudge: But what are assimilation and integration, and why does suppressing diversity often fail?

learn.hook: On an Indian currency note, the value is printed in more than a dozen languages. That small detail tells you how India chose to handle diversity.
points: India's diversity: over 121 crore people (Census 2011), very many languages and dialects, 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule, and all major world religions.

Census 2011 religious composition: Hindus about 79.8 per cent, Muslims about 14.2 per cent, Christians about 2.3 per cent, Sikhs about 1.7 per cent, Buddhists about 0.7 per cent and Jains about 0.4 per cent.
Minorities are distributed unevenly: e.g. Sikhs are a majority in Punjab, and Christians are a majority in Nagaland, Mizoram and Meghalaya.
India is described as a 'state-nation' rather than a nation-state: it seeks unity with diversity and allows multiple, complementary identities (one can be Tamil, Muslim and Indian at once).
The Constitution is secular but does not banish religion or language from public life; India follows neither assimilation nor integration. Problems arise mainly in implementation.

example.q: Using Census 2011, estimate the combined share of Hindus and Muslims in India's population.
steps: Hindus about 79.8 per cent.
Muslims about 14.2 per cent.
example.answer: About 94 per cent.

learn.reallife: A Kannadiga software engineer can speak Kannada at home, follow her religion, cheer for India in cricket and work in English: multiple complementary identities in one person.

teach.praise: India is a 'state-nation' that lets you be many things at once, with 22 scheduled languages and a Constitution that welcomes diversity!
teach.nudge: But what makes India's model different from forcing everyone into one culture?

learn.hook: In December 1952, Potti Sriramulu died after a long fast demanding a Telugu-speaking state. Within days, the government agreed. Language had redrawn India's map.
points: Regionalism in India is rooted in the geographical concentration of diverse languages, cultures, tribes and religions, and is encouraged by a sense of regional deprivation.
At independence, British India's large multilingual presidencies (Madras, Bombay, Bengal) and princely states were reorganised. Demands for linguistic states grew.

Potti Sriramulu's fast unto death (1952) led to the creation of Andhra state in 1953. The States Reorganisation Commission led to the States Reorganisation Act of 1956, which redrew boundaries on linguistic lines.
Linguistic states strengthened, rather than weakened, Indian unity, by giving language communities a stake in the nation.
Contrast: Sri Lanka's 'Sinhala only' language policy alienated Tamils and fed civil war; imposing Urdu on East Pakistan contributed to Pakistan's break-up and the birth of Bangladesh (1971).

example.q: Why does the book argue that linguistic states helped India's unity?
steps: Each major language community got its own state and a share in power.
This reduced fears of domination by another language.
Communities felt accommodated, so loyalty to the nation grew.
In contrast, imposing one language elsewhere caused conflict.
example.answer: Accommodating languages through states built trust and unity.

learn.reallife: Telangana, formed in 2014 from Andhra Pradesh, shows that regional identity and a sense of deprivation can create new states even within one language group.

topics.title: New states and federalism as accommodation

learn.hook: In November 2000, three new states appeared on India's map within weeks. Unlike 1956, language was not the reason.
points: In 2000, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand were formed. The basis was not language but a combination of tribal identity, regional deprivation and ecology.
Federalism is a key way to accommodate regional sentiments. The Constitution divides subjects into the Union List, State List and Concurrent List.
The Rajya Sabha represents the states in Parliament.
The Finance Commission recommends how tax revenues are shared between the Centre and states; the GST Council brings the Centre and states together to decide Goods and Services Tax rates.
Activity: research how your own state was formed and whether there are current demands for new states.

example.q: Which institutions help accommodate regional interests in Indian federalism, and how?
steps: Three lists divide powers so states control many subjects.
Rajya Sabha gives states a voice in Parliament.
Finance Commission shares revenue fairly.
GST Council makes Centre and states decide tax rates together.
example.answer: Union/State/Concurrent Lists, Rajya Sabha, Finance Commission and GST Council.

learn.reallife: Every GST Council meeting brings the Union Finance Minister and state finance ministers to one table, federalism in action.

quiz.explain: Shared and divided powers give regions a stake.

options: The demographic transition of her state's population

quiz.explain: Tracing state formation and new-state demands shows how regional identities arise and how federalism accommodates them.
quiz.mistake: Does not link state formation to regionalism and federalism

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why were new states formed in 2000, and how does federalism keep regions happy?'
teach.praise: So 2000's new states came from tribal identity, deprivation and ecology, and federal institutions share power and money with regions. Fair play!
teach.nudge: But on what basis were the 2000 states formed, and which federal institutions accommodate regions?

learn.hook: Parsis are among India's most economically successful communities, yet as a tiny group they worry about preserving their culture. In sociology, 'minority' is not just about numbers.
points: India's nationalism, shaped by the freedom struggle, aimed to be inclusive and democratic. Gandhi and Tagore warned against narrow, exclusive nationalism.
Sociologically, a minority is not just a small number; it implies some disadvantage, and members usually share a sense of group solidarity.
Some minorities are economically privileged, such as Parsis or many Sikhs, but may still face cultural disadvantage as small groups in a society dominated by a majority.
B.R. Ambedkar argued that the majority has a duty not to discriminate, and that protecting minorities is essential to keeping the nation united.

Articles 29 and 30: minorities have the right to conserve their distinct language, script or culture (Art. 29) and to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice (Art. 30). Forced imposition of a dominant culture weakens unity, as Bangladesh (1971) and Sri Lanka show.

example.q: Why are Parsis considered a minority in the sociological sense despite their prosperity?
steps: They are numerically very small.
As a small group they face cultural disadvantage: preserving language, rituals and customs is hard.
They share strong group solidarity.
example.answer: Numbers plus cultural disadvantage and solidarity make them a minority.

learn.reallife: Thousands of minority-run schools and colleges across India, set up by religious and linguistic minorities, rely on the rights protected by Article 30.

games.title: Match the idea
pairs: Right to conserve language, script or culture
Right to set up educational institutions
Small number plus disadvantage and solidarity

games.title: Minority check

It also involves disadvantage and group solidarity.
Economically privileged minorities may still face cultural disadvantage.
Parsis are an example.
Article 30 allows minorities to establish educational institutions.
That is the right under Article 30.
Ambedkar opposed any protection for minorities.
He argued protection was essential for unity.
Forced imposition of a dominant culture tends to strengthen national unity.
It weakens unity, as in Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

quiz.q: In sociology, a minority group is characterised by:
options: Only having fewer members than other groups
Always being poorer than all other groups
Living together in only one region of a country

quiz.explain: Numbers alone do not make a sociological minority.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a privileged minority facing cultural disadvantage?
options: The majority community
Dominant landowning castes

Parsis
quiz.explain: Parsis are prosperous but culturally a small minority.

options: Move freely and reside in any part of India
Conserve a distinct language, script or culture
Equality before the law for all persons alike
Contest elections to Parliament and assemblies
quiz.explain: Article 29 protects cultural and educational rights of minorities.

options: Form separate states of their own in India
Have their own separate courts of law

quiz.explain: Article 30 covers minority educational institutions.

quiz.q: Ambedkar argued that protecting minorities is necessary for:

Keeping the nation united

Creating separate nations
quiz.explain: He saw minority protection as a foundation of unity.

quiz.q: Gandhi and Tagore are cited in the book for:
options: Supporting assimilation of minorities
Criticising exclusive, narrow nationalism
Writing the States Reorganisation Act
Leading the Tebhaga movement
quiz.explain: Both favoured an inclusive vision of the nation.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Forced imposition of a dominant culture can weaken a nation.

options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: The Bangladesh case shows imposition leads to alienation and division.

quiz.q: Why does Indian nationalism aim to be inclusive?
options: It was imposed on India by its colonial rulers
It was based on a single religion and no other
It grew from a freedom struggle uniting many groups
It rejected democracy right from the very start
quiz.explain: The national movement brought diverse groups together.
quiz.mistake: Misreads the roots of Indian nationalism

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Isn't a minority just a small group? Why do minorities need special protection?'
teach.praise: So a minority has numbers, disadvantage and solidarity, and protecting it through Articles 29 and 30 keeps the nation united!
teach.nudge: But what makes a group a minority in sociology, and how does the Constitution protect minorities?

learn.hook: Kabir's dohas, sung in both temples and dargahs, mocked the walls people built between faiths. Communalism builds those walls higher; secularism tries to keep doors open.
points: Communalism, in India, means aggressive chauvinism based on religious identity. It is a political ideology, quite different from personal piety or devotion.
Communalism treats religious identity as overriding all others (language, class, region), and sees each religious group as homogeneous, ignoring internal differences.
India has a long history of communal riots: some pre-colonial conflicts, colonial 'divide and rule' policies that hardened identities, and post-independence riots involving almost all communities.
India also has strong traditions of pluralism and syncretism: the Bhakti and Sufi movements, and poets like Kabir, cut across religious boundaries.

Secularism has two senses: the Western sense of separation of church and state (linked to rationality and modernity), and the Indian sense of equal respect for all religions. In India, secularism is the opposite of communalism. Debates continue over minority protection versus charges of 'appeasement' or vote-bank politics.
Activity: collect stories, songs and memories of religious harmony from grandparents and elders in your neighbourhood, to see how syncretic traditions live on in everyday life.

example.q: A devout person visits a temple daily but has friends of all faiths and opposes violence. Is this communalism?
steps: Personal piety is religious devotion.
Communalism is an aggressive political ideology that treats religious identity as overriding and other groups as enemies.
This person shows piety without chauvinism.
example.answer: No. Piety is not communalism.

learn.reallife: Dargahs such as Ajmer Sharif and Nizamuddin draw visitors of many faiths, a living example of India's syncretic traditions.

options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A

quiz.explain: The distinction between devotion and political chauvinism explains A.

quiz.explain: Debate continues over minority protection and vote-bank charges.

quiz.explain: Elders' memories of shared festivals, shrines and songs show pluralism and syncretism at the local level.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Isn't communalism just people loving their religion? And what does secularism mean in India?'
teach.praise: So communalism is an aggressive political ideology, not devotion, and Indian secularism means equal respect for all faiths. Kabir would approve!
teach.nudge: But how is communalism different from being religious, and what are the two meanings of secularism?

topics.title: Authoritarian state, civil society and the RTI

learn.hook: In the 1990s, villagers in Rajasthan held public hearings where officials had to read out how money for local works was spent. Their slogan, roughly 'our money, our accounts', grew into a national law: the Right to Information Act.
points: An authoritarian state is the opposite of a democratic one: people have no voice, rulers are not accountable, and civil liberties such as freedom of press, speech and assembly are often curtailed.
The Emergency (June 1975 to March 1977), when civil liberties were suspended, taught Indians the value of democratic rights.

Civil society is the broad arena beyond the private family but outside both the state and the market: the public sphere of voluntary associations such as political parties, media, trade unions, NGOs, religious organisations and citizens' groups.
Civil society groups have taken up tribal land rights, campaigns against violence (including against women), displacement by dams, rights of slum dwellers and education.

The Right to Information Act, 2005 began with a grassroots campaign in Rajasthan (the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan's public hearings). It lets citizens demand information from public authorities within a fixed time, increasing transparency and accountability.

example.q: Classify: (a) a district collector's office, (b) a mobile phone company, (c) an NGO running night schools for working children.
steps: (a) Part of the government: the state.
(b) A profit-making business: the market.
(c) A non-state, non-profit voluntary body: civil society.
example.answer: (a) state; (b) market; (c) civil society.

learn.reallife: Students often file RTI applications to see their own evaluated answer sheets or to ask about delays in scholarships, using the 2005 Act directly.

options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A

quiz.explain: Losing liberties made people value them.

quiz.explain: Citizens can demand information from public bodies.

teach.praise: So civil society sits between family, state and market, it was crucial after the Emergency, and Rajasthan's villagers sparked the RTI Act of 2005!
teach.nudge: But what is civil society, and how did the RTI movement begin?

chapters.title: Indian Society: Suggestions for Project Work

topics.title: Choosing a method: surveys, interviews, observation

learn.hook: Want to know how many students in your school use the metro? Ask a hundred of them. Want to know how it feels to be the only girl in a physics tuition batch? Sit down and talk to a few. Different questions need different methods.
points: This chapter is non-evaluative in the CBSE 2026-27 theory paper, but it supports the 20-mark project. Its purpose is to give you first-hand experience of doing a small piece of sociological research.
The research question decides the method. There is no single 'best' method; each suits some questions better than others.
Survey: collecting the same information from many people, often with a questionnaire (a fixed list of written questions). Good for patterns and numbers.
Interview: a conversation with a respondent. Structured interviews follow fixed questions; open-ended (unstructured) interviews let the respondent talk freely and give depth.
Observation: participant observation (the researcher joins in the activity being studied) or non-participant observation (the researcher watches without taking part).

example.q: Which method suits each question? (a) What share of Class 12 students use coaching? (b) How do domestic workers experience their employers' homes? (c) How do people use a bus stop at rush hour?
steps: (a) Needs numbers from many people: survey with a questionnaire.
(b) Needs depth and feelings: open-ended interviews.
(c) Needs watching behaviour: observation.
example.answer: (a) survey; (b) interviews; (c) observation.

learn.reallife: Organisations like the NSSO run giant surveys of lakhs of households, while journalists often use long interviews; your project can borrow either style on a small scale.

games.title: Best method for the question
items: How many families own a two-wheeler?
What percentage of students walk to school?

options: Teach statistical formulas and nothing else at all
Replace the whole theory syllabus with projects
Give first-hand experience of small-scale research

quiz.explain: It introduces students to doing research themselves.

quiz.q: What decides which research method to use?
options: The research question
The researcher's favourite method
The cheapest method

quiz.explain: Methods are chosen to fit the question.

quiz.q: A survey is best suited for:
options: Studying one person's life story in great depth
Collecting the same information from many people
Joining a group's daily activities for months
Reading old letters kept in an archive
quiz.explain: Surveys gather comparable data across many respondents.
quiz.mistake: Confuses survey with interview or observation

quiz.q: In participant observation, the researcher:
options: Only reads documents and old records
Sends written questionnaires by post
Watches from a hidden camera only
Takes part in the activity being studied
quiz.explain: The researcher joins in to understand from inside.

quiz.q: An open-ended interview is useful because it:
options: Lets respondents explain in their own words
Uses only short yes-or-no questions
Gives quick numbers for very large groups
Needs no conversation with anyone at all
quiz.explain: It yields depth and meaning.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with a structured questionnaire

quiz.q: Which is a non-participant observation?
options: Working a week as a tea-stall helper to study it
Watching how commuters board a crowded bus
Joining a dance troupe to study it
Playing in a local cricket team to study it
quiz.explain: The researcher only watches, without joining.
quiz.mistake: Picks examples where the researcher participates

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): There is no single best method in sociology.
Reason (R): Different research questions call for different methods.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Because questions differ, the right method differs.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one method is always superior

quiz.q: The CBSE Sociology project carries how many marks?
quiz.explain: The project is worth 20 marks; the theory paper 80.

teach.ask: Gappu holds a clipboard: 'I want to research my school canteen. Should I do a survey, an interview or just watch?'
teach.praise: So the question decides the method: surveys for numbers, interviews for depth, observation for behaviour. Clipboard ready!
teach.nudge: But how do I choose between methods? What does each one do best?

topics.title: Other sources, mixed methods, ethics and the project file

learn.hook: An old family wedding album can tell you how dress, guests and rituals have changed over 50 years. Sociologists use photographs, letters, newspapers and records as data too.
points: Archives, old documents, photographs, letters, newspapers and other media are valuable sources, especially for studying change over time.
Combining methods (mixed methods), such as a survey plus a few interviews, gives a fuller picture than any single method.
Ethics: get informed consent, respect privacy and confidentiality, avoid harm, and treat respondents with respect. Never publish names or details without permission.
A project report usually has: introduction, statement of purpose, research question, methodology (methods and sample), data analysis, and conclusion.
The project is followed by a viva voce, an oral discussion where you explain what you did and what you found.

example.q: Arrange the parts of a project report in a sensible order.
steps: Introduction and statement of purpose.
Research question.
Methodology: how data were collected.
Data analysis.
Conclusion.
example.answer: Introduction → purpose → question → methodology → analysis → conclusion.

learn.reallife: Many families have photos from the 1970s onwards; comparing them with today's wedding photos is a quick, ethical archive project, as long as you have permission to use them.

teach.nudge: But what other sources can I use, and what ethics must I follow?

learn.hook: Who gets to sit on the bench at a bus stop? Who cooks and who washes up at home? Who appears on the front page of the newspaper? Everyday life is full of research questions.
points: Public use of space: who uses streets, parks, bus stops and markets, at what times, and how gender, age and class shape their use.
Media: how the content of newspapers or television has changed over time, e.g. which topics and groups get coverage.
Households and domestic work: who does what at home, and how the division of labour is gendered.
Transport: modes of travel (walking, cycle, bus, metro, car) and their social aspects, such as cost, safety and who uses which mode.

Life histories of people, places or everyday objects (e.g. the life of a cycle-rickshaw puller, a neighbourhood, or the pressure cooker). Students may also choose other local themes linked to the book.

example.q: Design a mini-project on domestic work in your neighbourhood.
steps: Question: who does cooking, cleaning and child care in 20 households?
Method: a short survey plus two open-ended interviews.
Ethics: take consent; do not record names.
Analysis: compare tasks done by men, women and children; draw a conclusion.
example.answer: A clear question, suitable methods, ethics and analysis make a sound project.

learn.reallife: Delhi Metro's women-only coaches and the debate around them are a ready-made project theme on gender and public space.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What topics can I pick for my sociology project? Something from daily life?'

teach.nudge: But which themes does the book suggest, and how do they connect to sociology?

learn.hook: You drive on the left, sit exams in English-medium formats, and go to courts with judges in black robes. Each of these is a small colonial legacy hiding in plain sight.
points: Colonialism had a contradictory impact on India: it brought liberal ideas such as democracy, equality and rights, but under an illiberal, undemocratic colonial rule.
This chapter focuses on two structural changes, industrialisation and urbanisation, in both colonial and independent India.
Everyday legacies of colonialism include the parliamentary, legal and police systems; the structure of schools; driving on the left side of the road; and many food habits and styles of dress.
English, introduced by colonial rule, is today both an advantage (access to jobs and global opportunities) and a marker of privilege (those without it are disadvantaged).

example.q: How is English an example of colonialism's contradictory legacy?
steps: English came with colonial rule, which was undemocratic.
Today it opens doors to jobs, higher education and global markets.
But those who cannot speak it are disadvantaged, so it also marks privilege.
example.answer: English is both a resource and a source of inequality.

learn.reallife: Indian IT firms owe part of their global success to English skills, yet many bright students from Hindi- or Odia-medium schools feel shut out of interviews conducted only in English.

games.title: Colonial legacy or not?
items: Parliamentary system

games.title: Contradictions of colonialism

learn.hook: Earlier conquerors in India often took tribute and settled down. The British East India Company did something new: it reorganised land, crops, forests and labour to feed British factories.
points: Colonialism is the rule of one country over another. Earlier empires also conquered, but modern (capitalist) colonialism was far more transformative.

Pre-capitalist conquerors mainly extracted tribute and left the economic structure largely intact. British colonialism, based on capitalism, interfered deeply to restructure the colony's economy for the benefit of Britain.

Colonial interventions: changing land ownership laws (new property rights and revenue systems), deciding which crops were grown (e.g. indigo, cotton), controlling forests, and organising labour for mines and plantations.
The aim was to make India a supplier of raw materials and a market for British manufactured goods.

example.q: How did British colonialism differ from earlier conquests of India?
steps: Earlier rulers mostly took tribute and did not remake production.

example.answer: It transformed the economic base instead of just collecting tribute.

topics.title: Colonialism and the movement of people

learn.hook: Today there are Indian-origin communities in Fiji, Mauritius, Trinidad and Guyana. Many trace their roots to ancestors who boarded ships as indentured labourers in the 19th century.
points: Colonialism moved people on a large scale. Labourers were taken to tea plantations in Assam, and as indentured labour to plantations abroad, e.g. Mauritius, Fiji and the Caribbean.
Indenture was a contract system binding labourers to work for a fixed period, often under very harsh conditions.

Middle-class professionals (lawyers, doctors, clerks, teachers, engineers) also moved within India to work in colonial administration and new institutions, e.g. many Bengalis and Tamils worked in distant provinces.
Western education created a new middle class. Ironically, this educated class became a key source of nationalist consciousness.

steps: Labour: workers recruited to Assam tea gardens or to plantations in Fiji.

example.answer: Tea garden or indentured labour, and professionals moving for colonial jobs.

learn.reallife: Mauritius and Fiji have strong Bhojpuri and Hindi traditions today, a legacy of indentured migration from eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

learn.hook: Western Europe's rise to global power was fuelled by voyages of exploration, plunder of colonies and the scientific revolution. Capitalism and colonialism grew up together.
points: Capitalism is an economic system in which the means of production are privately owned and organised to earn profit through the market. It is dynamic, always seeking new markets and resources.
Western capitalism had its origins in exploration of the world, plunder of its wealth and resources, and an unprecedented growth of science and technology.
Capitalism and colonialism were closely linked: colonies supplied raw materials, markets and investment opportunities.
The nation-state became the dominant modern political form. Ideas of nationhood and self-rule (swaraj) spread, and Indian nationalists demanded independence.
Indian nationalists exposed the contradiction between Britain's claims of liberalism and democracy at home and its undemocratic, exploitative rule in India.

example.q: Why did Indian nationalists say British liberalism was hypocritical?
steps: Britain praised liberty and democracy for its own citizens.
In India it ruled without consent and denied basic rights.
So its liberal claims did not apply to its colonies.
example.answer: Britain preached liberty at home but practised domination in India.

learn.reallife: Dadabhai Naoroji's 'drain of wealth' argument used British statistics to show how India's wealth flowed to Britain, an early nationalist critique of colonial capitalism.

learn.hook: In Britain, industrialisation emptied villages and filled cities. In colonial India, the opposite often happened: weavers lost work, old towns shrank, and people went back to the land.
points: Industrialisation is the emergence of machine production based on non-human power (steam, electricity). It is usually linked with urbanisation, as factories draw workers into towns.
In Britain, the first industrial nation, industrialisation led to a rapid shift of people from villages to cities.

In colonial India, there was deindustrialisation: cheap British machine-made goods destroyed India's artisanal manufacture (e.g. textiles). Old manufacturing and trading towns such as Surat and Masulipatnam declined, and court towns lost their patrons as Indian rulers lost power.
Displaced artisans were pushed back into agriculture, increasing pressure on land. A weak colonial middle class grew.
Census reports of the early 20th century, such as that of 1911, recorded village artisans abandoning their hereditary crafts.

example.q: Why did industrialisation in Britain lead to urbanisation, while in colonial India many artisans moved back to farming?
steps: Britain: new factories in cities needed workers, so villagers moved to towns.
India: British factory goods flooded Indian markets.
Indian artisans lost their livelihoods; with few new factories, they turned to agriculture.
example.answer: Britain industrialised; colonial India deindustrialised.

learn.reallife: Handloom clusters such as those of Varanasi, Bhagalpur or Chanderi still struggle with competition from power looms, an echo of the colonial deindustrialisation story.

learn.hook: Kolkata began as three small villages on the Hooghly. Within two centuries it was the capital of British India and one of the world's great port cities.
points: The colonial port cities of Bombay, Calcutta and Madras grew as links between the colony (the periphery) and Britain (the core of global capitalism).
They were concrete expressions of global capitalism: raw materials such as cotton, jute and indigo were collected and shipped out, and British manufactured goods came in.
Calcutta grew from three villages (Sutanati, Gobindapur and Kalikata) whose rights were acquired by the East India Company in the late 17th century. Fort William was built there.
Colonial cities were divided: a European 'white town' with spacious bungalows and a native 'black town' that was crowded and poorly serviced.
Many colonial city names were later changed, e.g. Bombay to Mumbai, Madras to Chennai, Calcutta to Kolkata.

example.q: Explain why Bombay, Calcutta and Madras were called 'links' between core and periphery.
steps: Core: Britain, the centre of industry.
Periphery: India, supplier of raw materials and market for goods.
Port cities handled the flow: cotton, jute and indigo out; machine goods in.
example.answer: They were the hubs through which colonial trade connected India to Britain.

learn.hook: A cup of Assam tea is a daily pleasure. Its history includes workers lured with false promises to remote estates, where the law stood firmly on the side of the planter.
points: The tea industry in Assam grew from the 1850s and needed huge amounts of labour to clear forests and work the gardens.
Labourers were recruited, often from distant regions, by fraud and coercion: false promises of good wages, and harsh treatment once they arrived.
Working conditions were very hard: low wages, long hours, disease and almost no freedom to leave.

Colonial laws backed planters: the Transport of Native Labourers Act of 1863 and its amendments regulated recruitment in ways that protected planters' interests, and made it hard for workers to escape.
The planters lived in luxury, with large bungalows, clubs and servants, a stark contrast with the misery of the labourers.

example.q: Why does the book use Assam tea gardens as an example of colonial capitalism?
steps: Tea was produced for profit and export.

example.answer: It shows how colonial capitalism combined profit, coercion and state support.

learn.reallife: Tea garden workers of Assam, many descended from migrants from Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh, still campaign for better wages and land rights.

learn.hook: Steel towns like Bhilai and Rourkela were built almost from scratch in the 1950s. For a newly independent nation, factories were symbols of self-reliance.
points: Economic exploitation was a central grievance of nationalists. The Swadeshi movement urged Indians to use Indian-made goods and boycott British ones.
After independence, leaders saw rapid industrialisation as the path to economic growth and social justice.
Planned development through Five-Year Plans emphasised heavy industry and the public sector, within a mixed economy (public and private sectors together).
New industrial townships grew around public sector plants, e.g. Bhilai, Bokaro, Rourkela and Durgapur.
Cooperative models such as Amul (in Gujarat) and Operation Flood showed another route, linking millions of small milk producers into a national network.

example.q: How did Amul and Operation Flood differ from steel plants as a development model?
steps: Steel plants: large, state-owned heavy industry in new townships.
Amul: cooperatives owned by small milk producers.
Operation Flood: linked rural cooperatives to urban markets nationally.
example.answer: One was state-led heavy industry; the other farmer-owned cooperative development.
