learn.hook: Gurugram's glass towers stand where wheat fields and villages stood forty years ago. Some villages have been swallowed by the city; others send their sons to distant cities and live on remittances.
points: Urbanisation has been rapid since independence: the urban share of the population rose from about 17 per cent in 1951 to about 31 per cent in 2011.
M.S.A. Rao described three situations of urban impact on villages.
Situation 1: villages that send many migrants to distant cities; remittances from them change the village economy and status.
Situation 2: villages located near a new industrial town, such as Bhilai, which draw workers into factory jobs and change village life.

Situation 3: villages swallowed by a growing metropolis, whose land is taken for housing and roads. Louis Wirth described 'urbanism as a way of life': large, dense, diverse populations produce impersonal, anonymous relations.

Is your place a village, town or city? The Census treats a place as a town if it has a municipality, or at least 5,000 people, a density of at least 400 per sq km and at least 75 per cent of male workers outside agriculture. Sociologically, also ask how large, dense and diverse it is, what work people do and how impersonal life is.

example.q: The urban share of India's population was about 17 per cent in 1951 and about 31 per cent in 2011. By how many percentage points did it rise?
steps: = 14 percentage points.
example.answer: About 14 percentage points.

learn.reallife: Many villages in Kerala live on remittances from the Gulf (Rao's first situation), while villages around Gurugram and Noida have been absorbed into the city (the third).

learn.hook: The sari worn with a blouse and petticoat feels completely 'traditional' today. Yet that combination became common only in the colonial period. Tradition, it turns out, keeps being reinvented.
points: Cultural change came through deliberate social reform movements and through less deliberate processes.
Four processes are studied: Sanskritisation (which began before colonialism), Westernisation, Modernisation and Secularisation.
Tradition is not fixed; it is living and constantly reinterpreted. Colonial modernity was paradoxical: it produced unintended cultural changes.
The four processes overlap and vary by region. One person can be modern in some ways and traditional in others, e.g. a software engineer who consults horoscopes for marriage.

Ideas of equality and democracy, spread in the colonial period, led people to reinterpret their own traditions. Example: the sari worn with blouse and petticoat became the new 'traditional' dress of the middle class.

example.q: Why is the blouse-and-petticoat sari an example of colonial modernity?
steps: Before colonial times, the sari was often worn without a blouse or petticoat in many regions.
Under colonial influence, middle-class women adopted the blouse and petticoat.
This new style came to be seen as 'traditional'.
So tradition was reinvented through modern influence.
example.answer: It shows tradition being reinterpreted under colonial modernity.

learn.reallife: A Bengaluru techie may code all day, do yoga in the evening and follow a priest's advice for a griha pravesh: modern and traditional at once.

teach.praise: Tradition keeps changing, colonial modernity was full of surprises, and a person can be modern and traditional together!
teach.nudge: But what are the four processes, and how can tradition be reinvented?

topics.title: Social reform: issues and new modes of change

learn.hook: When Rammohun Roy argued against sati in the 1810s and 1820s, his pamphlets were printed and read across Bengal. Earlier saints had preached against discrimination too; what changed was the printing press.
points: 19th-century reformers targeted sati, child marriage, the ban on widow remarriage, caste discrimination and denial of education to women.
Challenges to social discrimination were not new: Buddhism, the Bhakti and Sufi movements had earlier questioned caste and ritual. The new feature was the modern context and means.
Satish Saberwal identified three aspects of modern change in colonial India: modes of communication, forms of organisation, and the nature of ideas.
Modes of communication: the printing press, telegraph and later the microphone; movement of people and goods through railways and steamships spread ideas quickly.
Forms of organisation: modern associations such as the Brahmo Samaj in Bengal, the Arya Samaj in Punjab and the All-India Muslim Ladies Conference; newspapers and journals spread debates.

example.q: Classify each under Saberwal's aspects: (a) the printing press; (b) the Arya Samaj; (c) liberal ideas of rights.
steps: (a) A means of spreading messages: modes of communication.
(b) A modern association: forms of organisation.
(c) New thinking: nature of ideas.
example.answer: (a) communication; (b) organisation; (c) ideas.

learn.reallife: Just as the printing press and telegraph spread reform debates in the 1800s, social media spreads campaigns today, a modern 'mode of communication'.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Reformers fought sati and caste. But saints did that before too. What was new?'
teach.praise: What was new was the modern toolkit: printing, telegraph, railways, new associations and new ideas. Saberwal's three aspects!
teach.nudge: But what did Saberwal say was new about modern reform?

learn.hook: Reformers rarely said 'tradition is bad, follow the West.' Instead they argued: 'Read our own scriptures properly and you will find support for reform.' That double strategy made them persuasive.
points: Reform ideas mixed Western liberalism (natural rights, reason, equality) with new readings of Indian tradition.
Raja Rammohun Roy attacked sati using both humanitarian, natural-rights arguments and Hindu scriptures.

M.G. Ranade's writings cited scriptures to show that widow remarriage had religious sanction. Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar also wrote in favour of widow remarriage (the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act was passed in 1856).
Sir Syed Ahmed Khan interpreted Islam by stressing free enquiry (ijtihad) and argued that it was compatible with modern science and the laws of nature.

Kandukuri Viresalingam (Andhra) drew on classical Indian logic (navya-nyaya) for reform. Jyotiba Phule opened one of the first schools for girls in Pune and argued for a pre-Aryan 'golden age' before Brahmanical dominance.

example.q: How did Rammohun Roy build his case against sati?
steps: He used Western ideas of humanity and natural rights.
He also cited Hindu scriptures to show sati was not required.
Combining both made the case harder for opponents to dismiss.
example.answer: He combined natural rights with scriptural arguments.

learn.reallife: Savitribai Phule, who taught in the Phules' school for girls, is remembered as a pioneer woman teacher; Maharashtra marks her birth anniversary, 3 January, as Balika Din.

topics.title: Differences within reform and orthodox opposition

learn.hook: When reformers campaigned to end sati, a group of orthodox Hindus formed the Dharma Sabha in Calcutta to oppose them. Reform always meets resistance, and reformers themselves often disagreed.
points: Reform was not one unified movement. Upper-caste reformers often focused on issues like widow remarriage and women's education, while Dalit and lower-caste reformers focused on caste discrimination and dignity.
Some Dalit thinkers rejected Hinduism altogether rather than reforming it.
Among Muslim women, Jahanara Shah Nawaz moved a resolution against polygamy at the All-India Muslim Ladies Conference; it was passed despite debate.
Orthodox groups opposed reform; the Dharma Sabha in Bengal petitioned against the abolition of sati.
Activity: study a reformer such as Pandita Ramabai, Sri Narayana Guru or Dayanand Saraswati.

example.q: Why might a Dalit reformer and an upper-caste reformer of the 19th century have had different priorities?
steps: Upper-caste women faced issues like enforced widowhood and seclusion.
Dalits faced untouchability and exclusion from temples, wells and schools.
So reform priorities depended on social position.
example.answer: Different social positions produced different reform agendas.

learn.reallife: Sri Narayana Guru's slogan 'one caste, one religion, one God for humankind' still inspires social movements in Kerala.

learn.hook: A caste that once ate meat turns vegetarian, starts wearing the sacred thread and invites Brahmin priests. M.N. Srinivas called this process Sanskritisation.
points: Sanskritisation (M.N. Srinivas): the process by which a 'low' caste, tribe or other group takes over the customs, rituals, beliefs, ideology and style of life of a high, often 'twice-born' (dwija) caste.

It varies by region: where a dominant caste is non-Brahmin (e.g. a landowning peasant caste), it may set the cultural model; in some regions, de-Sanskritisation occurs, where non-Sanskritic dominant castes are imitated.
Preconditions: improvement in economic or political position, or contact with the 'Great Tradition' (for example through a pilgrimage centre or religious institution).

Dominant castes often resisted lower castes' attempts to Sanskritise. Kumud Pawade, a Dalit woman who became a Sanskrit scholar, described the surprise and hostility she faced in studying and teaching Sanskrit.

example.q: A lower caste in a village becomes prosperous through trade. It then gives up meat and liquor and adopts Brahmin rituals. Explain using Srinivas.
steps: Economic improvement is a precondition.
Adopting the customs of a higher caste is Sanskritisation.
The aim is to claim higher ritual status.
example.answer: It is Sanskritisation, triggered by improved economic position.

learn.reallife: Debates over who may chant mantras or become a temple priest, still heard today, echo the resistance Kumud Pawade faced.

quiz.q: De-Sanskritisation refers to:
options: Giving up the study of Sanskrit texts in school
Abolition of the whole caste system by law
Imitation of non-Sanskritic dominant castes
Migration of a whole caste to a big city
quiz.explain: Where non-Sanskritic castes dominate, their culture becomes the model.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is Sanskritisation? Is it just learning Sanskrit?'
teach.praise: Not just Sanskrit! It's lower groups adopting higher-caste customs, often after gaining wealth, and dominant castes often resisted it.
teach.nudge: But what exactly is Sanskritisation, and when does it happen?

learn.hook: If a caste climbs one rung on the ladder, the ladder itself stays standing. That is the core criticism of Sanskritisation.
points: It exaggerates social mobility: it leads to positional change for some groups, not structural change. Inequality persists; some castes just move up within it.
It accepts the ideology of upper-caste superiority: imitating the upper castes implies that their way of life is better.
It justifies inequality and exclusion, since it accepts purity-pollution ideas and the hierarchy they support.
It harms women: Sanskritising castes often adopt seclusion of women and dowry, replacing bride-price, which lowers women's status.
It erodes Dalit culture and the dignity of their labour and crafts. Backward class movements and Dalit assertion have offered alternatives, rejecting rather than imitating upper-caste culture.

example.q: Write two points of a critical essay on Sanskritisation focusing on gender.
steps: Sanskritising castes often adopt seclusion and restrictions on women's mobility.
Bride-price, which gave value to brides, is replaced by dowry, which treats daughters as a burden.
So upward mobility of the caste can mean a decline in women's status.
example.answer: Seclusion and dowry worsen women's status.

learn.reallife: Dalit literature and art that celebrate Dalit culture, music and food reject the idea that one must imitate upper castes to gain dignity.

quiz.explain: Accepting purity-pollution ideas legitimises hierarchy.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If a lower caste moves up by Sanskritisation, isn't that progress? Why criticise it?'
teach.praise: So Sanskritisation shifts positions but not the ladder, accepts upper-caste superiority, hurts women and Dalit culture. Critique complete!
teach.nudge: But what are the main criticisms of Sanskritisation, especially for women and Dalits?

learn.hook: Raja Ravi Varma painted Hindu goddesses with European oil-painting techniques. Chandu Menon wrote a Malayalam novel inspired by English novels. Westernisation shaped art as much as dress.
points: Westernisation (M.N. Srinivas): the changes in Indian society and culture resulting from over 150 years of British rule, at levels such as technology, institutions, ideology and values.

Two kinds: a westernised sub-culture of a small elite who first came into contact with the West (some of them intellectuals with Western liberal values); and a general spread of Western traits such as new technology, dress and food.
Adopting Western forms (dress, gadgets) does not necessarily bring democratic or egalitarian values. Westernisation is not only about lifestyle.
Western influence on art and literature: Raja Ravi Varma's paintings, Abanindranath Tagore's art blending Indian and Western styles, Chandu Menon's Malayalam novel and Bankimchandra's Bengali novels.

Debate: it was once said upper castes westernise while lower castes Sanskritise, but some lower castes, such as the Thiyyas of Kerala, chose Westernisation. Westernisation can also cause generational conflict over dress and lifestyle.

example.q: A family uses smartphones and wears jeans but refuses to let its daughter choose her career. Is this full Westernisation?
steps: The family has adopted Western technology and dress.
But it has not adopted values such as individual choice and gender equality.
Westernisation of form does not guarantee Westernisation of values.
example.answer: No: Westernisation of lifestyle need not bring egalitarian values.

learn.reallife: Raja Ravi Varma's oleographs of gods and goddesses, printed on his own press, still decorate calendars in homes across India.

games.title: Match the Westernisation example
pairs: Art blending Indian and Western styles

Some lower castes chose Westernisation over Sanskritisation.

quiz.explain: Different attitudes to Western ways create friction.

quiz.explain: It is a broad, multi-level process.

teach.ask: Gappu wears tiny sunglasses: 'If I wear jeans and use a phone, am I westernised?'
teach.praise: Not just jeans! Westernisation covers technology, institutions, ideas and values, from Ravi Varma's art to the Thiyyas' choices.
teach.nudge: But is Westernisation only about dress? What kinds and levels does it include?

learn.hook: An engineer may be selected by an online exam on merit, yet her marriage may still be fixed within her caste. Modernisation in India rarely follows the textbook script.
points: Modernisation first referred to improvement in technology and production. Later it came to mean the path of development followed by Western Europe and North America, which others were expected to follow.

Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph described features of modernity: local ties give way to universal commitments; utility, calculation and science replace the sacred; the individual, not the group, becomes the unit of society; choice replaces birth in deciding one's place; achievement replaces ascription; and work is separated from home and family.
In India, modernisation has not erased tradition: caste-based occupations, endogamy and religion persist alongside modern schools, factories and offices.
So Indian modernity combines modern institutions with traditional practices.

example.q: Classify: (a) a job given through an open, merit-based exam; (b) a marriage arranged within the caste.
steps: (a) Achievement over ascription, choice over birth: a modern feature.
(b) Ascription and endogamy: a traditional feature.
Both can exist in the same family.
example.answer: (a) modern; (b) traditional; together, Indian modernity.

learn.reallife: UPSC and ISRO recruit through open competitive exams, an example of achievement replacing ascription.

options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A

quiz.explain: Status is achieved through choice rather than ascribed.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is modernisation? Does it mean India has left tradition behind?'
teach.praise: Modernisation means achievement over ascription, the individual as the unit and science over the sacred, but in India tradition persists alongside!
teach.nudge: But what features of modernity did the Rudolphs list, and does tradition disappear in India?

learn.hook: Big fat Indian weddings are religious ceremonies, but they are also showcases of wealth, networking events and photo shoots. That non-religious side of ritual is part of secularisation.
points: In the Western sense, secularisation means the declining influence of religion in society.
Rituals have secular dimensions: they offer occasions to display wealth and status, to socialise, and for men and women to meet and network. Weddings are a prime example.
Caste has also been secularised: it has moved away from purity-pollution ideas towards functioning as a political pressure group. Caste associations and caste-based parties bargain for resources.

Rajni Kothari argued that caste and politics shape each other: caste changes under the influence of democratic politics, as politics is shaped by caste. In his words, it is caste that gets politicised.

example.q: Write a note on rites and secularisation using a wedding.
steps: Religious side: rituals, priests, sacred fire.
Secular side: display of wealth, gifts, social networking, meeting relatives and potential partners.
Growing importance of the secular side shows secularisation of ritual.
example.answer: Weddings remain religious but increasingly serve secular purposes.

learn.reallife: Caste mahasabhas that hold conventions, issue manifestos and endorse candidates before elections show caste acting as a political pressure group.

quiz.explain: Caste functions as an interest group.

options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A

quiz.explain: Kothari's two-way relationship explains A.

quiz.explain: Caste's basis shifts from ritual to political interest.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If weddings are still full of rituals, how can we talk about secularisation?'

chapters.title: Social Change: Change and Development in Rural Society

topics.title: Agriculture, rural life and agrarian structure

learn.hook: Pongal, Bihu, Baisakhi and Ugadi are harvest or new-year festivals tied to the farming calendar. In rural India, agriculture is not just an occupation; it is a way of life.
points: Agriculture is the main source of livelihood for most rural Indians, and it shapes rural culture: many festivals such as Pongal (Tamil Nadu), Bihu (Assam), Baisakhi (Punjab) and Ugadi (Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh) mark the agricultural cycle.
Rural society is more than farming: it includes artisans (potters, carpenters, weavers), service castes (washermen, barbers) and growing non-farm work.
Agrarian structure refers to the distribution of land (who owns, who rents, who works it). It shapes rural class relations.
Rural classes: large landowners; middle and small farmers who cultivate their own land; tenants who rent land; and landless agricultural labourers who work for wages.

example.q: In a village, the Singh family owns 50 acres and hires workers; Ramu rents 3 acres; Sita works for daily wages on others' fields. Place each in the agrarian structure.
steps: Singh family: large landowners.
Ramu: tenant cultivator.
Sita: landless agricultural labourer.
example.answer: Landowner, tenant and landless labourer.

learn.reallife: During Baisakhi in Punjab, the wheat harvest is celebrated with bhangra; the fields themselves are owned and worked by people from very different classes.

quiz.explain: Land control creates class positions.

quiz.explain: Those with more land than they can work themselves hire labourers.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Isn't a village just a bunch of farmers? What is agrarian structure?'
teach.praise: So villages have landowners, tenants and landless labourers, plus artisans and service castes, and festivals follow the farming calendar!
teach.nudge: But how is land distributed in a village, and who else lives there besides farmers?

learn.hook: In many villages, a simple question, 'Who owns the land?', has the same answer as 'Which caste dominates?' Land and caste tend to go together.
points: There is a strong overlap of caste and land: dominant landowning castes include the Jats (Punjab, Haryana, western UP), Patidars (Gujarat), Reddis and Kammas (Andhra Pradesh), Vokkaligas (Karnataka) and Marathas (Maharashtra).
Most agricultural labourers belong to Dalit and lower castes, who were historically denied land ownership.
Women do a great deal of farm work, but have very limited rights to own land. Patrilineal inheritance usually passes land to sons.

Traditional dependency relations: the jajmani system, an exchange of services and goods between landowning and service castes; bonded labour, such as the Halpati system of Gujarat, where labourers were tied to landowning families for generations; and begar (forced, unpaid labour).

example.q: Why do most agricultural labourers in India come from Dalit and lower castes?
steps: Historically, these castes were denied land ownership.
Landowning was concentrated among upper and dominant castes.
Without land, people must work for wages on others' fields.
example.answer: Caste-based exclusion from land made them labourers.

learn.reallife: Studies of women farmers show that although they do most of the sowing, weeding and harvesting, land titles are mostly in men's names, which limits their access to loans.

teach.nudge: But how are caste and land linked, and what were the traditional dependency relations?

topics.title: Colonial land revenue and post-independence land reforms

learn.hook: When land ceiling laws were passed, some landlords suddenly 'divided' their estates among cousins and servants, or put them in false (benami) names. On paper the land was redistributed; in reality little changed.
points: Colonial land revenue systems: under the zamindari system (e.g. Bengal's Permanent Settlement) zamindars collected revenue from cultivators and paid a fixed sum to the British; under the ryotwari system (e.g. Madras and Bombay) cultivators paid revenue directly to the state. Zamindari areas later showed poorer agricultural development.
Land reforms after independence aimed to reduce rural inequality and increase agricultural productivity.
Abolition of the zamindari system removed intermediaries between the state and cultivators; it was the most successful land reform.
Tenancy abolition and regulation laws aimed to give tenants security or ownership. Land ceiling acts limited the maximum land a family could hold and redistributed the surplus.
Success was limited: landlords evaded laws through benami (false-name) transfers, dividing land among relatives and evicting tenants. Reforms were more effective in Kerala and West Bengal.

example.q: Why did land ceiling laws have limited success?
steps: Landlords transferred land to relatives or false names (benami).
They evicted tenants before laws took effect.
Weak political will and loopholes allowed evasion.
example.answer: Evasion through benami transfers, splitting land and eviction.

learn.reallife: West Bengal's Operation Barga recorded the names of sharecroppers so they could not be evicted, one reason land reforms were more effective there.

items: Intermediaries collect revenue

quiz.explain: They capped holdings and redistributed the excess.

quiz.q: 'Benami' transfers were used to:
options: Register land in the owner's own true name
Buy surplus land directly from the government
Evade land ceiling laws by using false names

quiz.explain: Land was put in others' names to escape ceilings.

quiz.explain: Political will made reforms more effective there.

options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A

A is true, but R is false

quiz.explain: Evasion undercut the reforms.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why didn't land reforms give land to everyone who works on it?'
teach.praise: So zamindari abolition worked best, but ceilings and tenancy laws were evaded through benami transfers, except where political will was strong.
teach.nudge: But what were the land reform measures, and why did some fail?

topics.title: The Green Revolution and its social consequences

learn.hook: In the mid-1960s India depended on food imports. Within a decade, Punjab's fields were producing record wheat harvests. But who gained, and who lost?
points: The Green Revolution, from the 1960s, introduced high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds of wheat and rice, along with fertilisers, pesticides and assured irrigation. It was concentrated in Punjab, western Uttar Pradesh, coastal Andhra Pradesh and parts of Tamil Nadu.
In the first phase, medium and large landowners who could afford the new inputs gained most; productivity rose sharply.
Tenants were often evicted as owners took land back for profitable cultivation; service castes lost work; mechanisation reduced demand for labour.
Regional inequality grew between Green Revolution areas and the rest. Agriculture became commercialised and dependent on markets for inputs and sales.
A second phase spread the technology to dry and rain-fed areas. Ecological costs included soil degradation and falling groundwater tables.

example.q: Why did large landowners benefit more than small farmers in the first phase?
steps: HYV seeds needed fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation, which cost money.
Large owners could afford inputs and take risks.
Small farmers had less capital and credit, so they gained less.
example.answer: The costly input package favoured those with land and capital.

learn.reallife: Punjab's falling water table, now among the fastest-declining in India, is one of the ecological costs of intensive Green Revolution farming.

quiz.explain: Concentration in some regions widened gaps.

quiz.q: Commercialisation of agriculture means farmers increasingly:
options: Grow food only for use at home

quiz.explain: Inputs are bought and output sold in markets.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'The Green Revolution grew lots of food. Wasn't it good for everyone?'
teach.praise: So it boosted output, but big landowners gained most, tenants and labourers lost out, regions grew unequal and the environment suffered.
teach.nudge: But who gained and who lost from the Green Revolution?

learn.hook: A grandfather worked for the same landlord family all his life and was paid in grain at harvest. His grandson works for whichever farmer pays the best daily wage in cash. That shift is a big change in rural society.
points: With commercialisation, labour relations shifted from patronage (long-term, personal ties, payment in kind) to contractual relations based on cash wages.
Capitalist farming developed: farmers produced for the market and reinvested profits. A new rural entrepreneurial class emerged.
Dominant castes invested their agricultural surplus in education, business (e.g. trading, transport, small industries) and politics, extending their power.
Traditional bonds weakened and the jajmani system declined, as cash payment replaced customary exchange.

example.q: Compare a patron-client labour relation with a contractual one.
steps: Patron-client: long-term, personal, often caste-based; payment in kind; obligations on both sides.
Contractual: short-term, impersonal; payment in cash wages; no wider obligations.
Commercial agriculture favours contractual relations.
example.answer: Patronage is personal and in kind; contract is impersonal and in cash.

learn.reallife: Farmer families from Andhra Pradesh and Punjab who started cinema halls, transport companies and engineering colleges show how agrarian surplus became business capital.

options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A

teach.nudge: But how did labour relations change, and what did dominant castes do with their surplus?

learn.hook: Every season, buses and trains carry thousands of workers from Bihar and Odisha to Punjab's farms, Gujarat's brick kilns and Mumbai's construction sites. They come and go, never quite settling anywhere.
points: Seasonal migration: agricultural labourers move for part of the year to prosperous farming regions (e.g. Punjab, Haryana) and to cities, then return home.
Jan Breman called such migrants 'footloose labour': they move from place to place without job security, often living in poor conditions.
Employers often prefer migrant labour because it is cheaper and easier to control than local labour, which may be organised or demand higher wages.
As men migrate, women increasingly take up farm work at home: the feminisation of agricultural labour.

example.q: Why might a Punjab farmer prefer migrant workers from Bihar over local labourers?
steps: Migrants may accept lower wages.
They are unorganised and far from home, so easier to control.
Local workers may demand higher wages or be unionised.
example.answer: Migrant labour is cheaper and more easily controlled.

learn.reallife: During the 2020 lockdown, images of migrant workers walking hundreds of kilometres home made the 'footloose labour' of India visible to everyone.

learn.hook: A farmer signs a contract with a company to grow a particular potato variety for chips. The company supplies seeds and promises to buy. What could go wrong?
points: Liberalisation since the 1990s has exposed Indian agriculture to world markets and prices.

Contract farming: companies decide what crops to grow, supply seeds and inputs, and agree to buy the produce. Farmers get assured buyers but bear risks: rejection of produce, dependence on one company and loss of control over their land use.
Multinational agribusiness companies have entered the market for seeds, fertilisers and pesticides.
This can erode local knowledge and biodiversity, as traditional seeds are replaced, and make farmers dependent on corporate inputs.
Agrarian distress and farmer suicides: since the late 1990s many farmers have taken their lives, due to debt, crop failure, falling prices and lack of support such as credit and insurance.

example.q: List the risks of contract farming for a small farmer.
steps: The company may reject produce for not meeting standards.
The farmer depends on one buyer and its prices.
Specialised crops reduce food security and local seed varieties.
Inputs bought from the company add to debt.
example.answer: Rejection, dependence, loss of biodiversity and debt.

learn.reallife: In 2019 a multinational snack company filed cases against some potato farmers in Gujarat over a registered variety, then withdrew them; the episode sparked debate about farmers' rights in a corporate seed market.

games.title: Benefit or risk of contract farming?
items: Assured buyer for the crop

quiz.explain: These input markets saw corporate entry.

options: Closing it to all kinds of foreign trade

teach.praise: Globalisation brought contract farming and corporate seeds, with risks of dependence, loss of local knowledge and debt that cause distress.
teach.nudge: But what are contract farming and corporate inputs, and why do they create risks?

chapters.title: Social Change: Change and Development in Industrial Society

learn.hook: In Charlie Chaplin's film 'Modern Times', a worker tightens bolts so fast on an assembly line that he is swallowed by the machine. It is comedy, but also a sharp image of industrial work.
points: Karl Marx argued that under industrial capitalism workers are alienated: they do not own what they produce, have no control over the work process, and their work gives them no satisfaction.
The assembly line breaks work into small repetitive tasks; the worker becomes like a part of the machine, an image captured in Chaplin's 'Modern Times'.
Industrialisation brings some equality: people of different castes travel together in trains and work side by side in offices and factories. But it also creates new inequalities of class and income.

Scientific management (Taylorism), developed by Frederick Winslow Taylor, broke tasks into the smallest parts and timed them to raise output. Henry Ford's assembly-line mass production (Fordism) applied this to cars.

example.q: Why might a worker who fixes the same bolt on 500 cars a day feel alienated, in Marx's sense?
steps: He does not own the cars he helps produce.
He has no say over the speed or design of the work.
The repetitive task gives no creative satisfaction.
example.answer: He is separated from the product, the process and meaningful work.

learn.reallife: Food-delivery riders whose routes, times and ratings are set by an app experience a modern form of the control Marx and Taylor would recognise.

games.title: Match the thinker or idea
pairs: Worker separated from product and process

On an assembly line, workers set their own pace freely.
The line sets the pace.

quiz.explain: It sought efficiency through fragmentation of work.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What did Marx mean by alienation? And what is this Taylorism?'
teach.praise: Marx said workers are alienated from product and process; Taylor and Ford broke work into timed, repetitive tasks. Chaplin showed it all!
teach.nudge: But what is alienation, and how did Taylor and Ford change work?

learn.hook: A bank clerk has a fixed salary, provident fund, paid leave and a pension. A construction worker on the same street may have none of these. Both are workers; their worlds are very different.
points: India's industrial pattern differs from the West: most workers are still in agriculture and the unorganised sector, not in large factories.

Organised (formal) sector: units employing ten or more people throughout the year, registered with the government, with regular jobs, fixed wages, benefits (provident fund, leave, pension) and union protection.
Unorganised (informal) sector: small units and self-employment, with irregular work, low wages, little job security and few legal protections. The vast majority of Indian workers are here.
In the early years after independence, the state led industrial development through the public sector, offering secure jobs to a small section of workers.

example.q: Classify: (a) a clerk in a public sector bank; (b) a street vendor; (c) a domestic worker; (d) a worker in a government steel plant.
steps: (a) Regular job with benefits: organised.
(b) Self-employed, no benefits: unorganised.
(c) No contract or benefits: unorganised.
(d) Public sector job with benefits: organised.
example.answer: (a) and (d) organised; (b) and (c) unorganised.

learn.reallife: e-Shram, the national database of unorganised workers, aims to bring crores of informal workers into the reach of social security schemes.

learn.hook: After 1991, India opened its doors to foreign companies and sold shares in public sector firms. Call centres boomed, but many factory jobs turned into short-term contracts.
points: Liberalisation and globalisation from 1991 included disinvestment (selling government shares in public sector units), privatisation, and the entry of multinational companies.
Firms increasingly outsourced work to smaller units or contractors, and hired contract workers instead of permanent staff.
This reduced job security: permanent jobs shrank in many sectors, and informal and contract work grew, even inside large factories.
Some new opportunities emerged, e.g. in IT and services, but mainly for the educated and skilled.

steps: Disinvestment or privatisation changed ownership.
New owners cut permanent staff and hired contract workers.
The worker faced less job security, or lost a permanent job.
example.answer: Job security fell as contract work replaced permanent employment.

learn.reallife: Many large factories today have more contract workers than permanent employees on the same assembly line.

quiz.explain: Contract hiring reduced security.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How did the 1991 reforms change jobs in India?'
teach.praise: After 1991, disinvestment and outsourcing grew, contract work replaced permanent jobs, and security fell for many. Skilled workers gained more.
teach.nudge: But what did liberalisation do to permanent jobs and job security?

learn.hook: Ask a construction worker in Mumbai how he got his job and he will probably name a mistri from his own village, not a job portal.
points: Most Indians are self-employed (e.g. farmers, shopkeepers, vendors) or do casual work.
Only a few find jobs through formal recruitment such as employment exchanges, advertisements and exams.
Contractors, jobbers and mistris recruit many workers, often from their own village or caste, and may control wages and conditions.
Social networks of kin, caste and region are crucial for getting jobs. In mills, 'badli' workers substituted for permanent workers on leave, hoping for permanent jobs later.

example.q: Why do workers in the unorganised sector rely so much on contractors and kin networks?
steps: Formal recruitment covers only a small share of jobs.
Contractors and kin provide information and introductions.
Trust and shared village or caste ties make networks important.
example.answer: Informal networks replace formal recruitment for most workers.

learn.reallife: Many delivery and security jobs in cities still spread by word of mouth among people from the same district, even when apps are involved.

teach.nudge: But how do most Indian workers actually find work?

learn.hook: In a modern car plant, a finished car can roll off the line every minute or less. Behind that speed lies a carefully designed system to control every second of a worker's time.
points: Managers aim to control workers and get more output from them.
Two main methods: lengthening the working day, or increasing the speed and intensity of work within the same hours. Machines and assembly lines set the pace.
Example of a car factory: tight shifts, very short breaks, constant pressure to keep up with the line, and high stress; workers may fall sick or burn out.
White-collar and IT work also involve long hours and tight deadlines. 'Flexible time' often means working late into the night to meet clients' schedules in other time zones.

example.q: A car factory worker gets two short tea breaks and must match the line's speed. Which method of control is at work?
steps: The working day is not necessarily longer.
But work intensity is raised by the line's speed.
So control works by increasing the speed of work.
example.answer: Control through increasing the speed and intensity of work.

learn.reallife: IT employees in Bengaluru often work on US time for project calls, an example of 'flexible' hours that stretch the working day.

learn.hook: A woman rolls a thousand bidis a day at home, paid a few rupees per hundred. A miner digs coal without proper safety gear. Both are workers whom labour laws often fail to reach.
points: Mines, quarries and many factories have hazardous conditions. Laws such as the Mines Act, 1952 set rules on hours, safety and welfare, but enforcement is often poor, especially in small and illegal units.
Contract workers in mines and construction often lack safety equipment, regular wages and benefits.
Accidents, occupational diseases (e.g. lung diseases from dust) and lack of compensation are common problems.
Home-based work: production done at home for traders or firms, such as bidi rolling, agarbatti making, papad rolling, zari and embroidery.
Home-based workers are mostly women and children, paid on piece rates (per unit produced), with no job security or benefits.

example.q: Why are home-based workers especially vulnerable?
steps: They work alone at home, so they are hard to organise.
They are paid per piece, often very low rates.
Labour laws rarely cover them, so they lack security and benefits.
example.answer: Isolation, piece rates and lack of legal protection.

learn.reallife: SEWA (Self-Employed Women's Association) in Ahmedabad has organised lakhs of home-based and informal women workers to bargain for better rates.

learn.hook: In January 1982, around two and a half lakh textile workers in Bombay went on strike. It lasted about two years, and many mills never reopened.
points: A strike is when workers stop work collectively to press their demands. A lockout is when management shuts the workplace to pressure workers.
Trade unions grew in India from the early 20th century and helped win better wages, hours and safety for organised workers.

The Bombay textile strike of 1982, led by trade union leader Datta Samant, involved around 2.5 lakh mill workers and lasted about two years. It ended in defeat: many mills closed and workers lost their jobs, often moving to informal work or returning to villages.
With informalisation and liberalisation, unions have weakened: contract and home-based workers are harder to organise, and many new firms resist unions.

example.q: Why did the Bombay textile strike end in loss for many workers?
steps: The strike lasted about two years, exhausting workers' savings.
Mill owners did not concede; many mills closed or shifted production.
Workers lost jobs and many moved into informal work.
example.answer: The prolonged strike led to mill closures and job losses.

learn.reallife: Many of central Mumbai's former mill compounds have been redeveloped as malls and offices, a physical reminder of the decline of the textile industry after 1982.

teach.nudge: But how are strikes and lockouts different, and why have unions weakened?

learn.hook: The eight-hour working day, the right to vote for women and laws against untouchability did not fall from the sky. Each was won by a social movement.
points: Social movements have shaped modern rights and institutions, e.g. labour laws, women's rights and anti-discrimination laws.
A social movement is a collective attempt to bring about change, or to resist it.
Features: sustained collective action over a period of time, not a one-off protest or riot.
Participants share objectives and an ideology: a common understanding of what is wrong and what should change.
There is some organisation: leadership and a structure for making decisions and planning action.

example.q: A crowd blocks a road for one afternoon after an accident and then disperses. Is this a social movement?
steps: It is collective, but not sustained over time.
There is no shared long-term ideology or organisation.
So it is a protest, not a social movement.
example.answer: No: it lacks sustained action, shared ideology and organisation.

learn.reallife: The campaign that produced the RTI Act lasted over a decade, had leaders and organisations, and a clear goal: a textbook social movement.

quiz.explain: Sustained, collective, purposeful action defines a movement.

quiz.explain: The lack of sustained action rules it out.

quiz.explain: Ideology unites members in purpose.

quiz.q: Which is the best example of a social movement?
options: A one-time protest at a local bus stop

A decades-long campaign for women's rights
quiz.explain: It is sustained, organised and ideological.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Is every protest a social movement?'
teach.praise: No! A social movement needs sustained collective action, shared ideology and some organisation. One-day protests don't count.
teach.nudge: But what features make something a social movement rather than just a protest?

learn.hook: When Rammohun Roy campaigned against sati, the Dharma Sabha campaigned to keep it. Every movement can spark a counter-movement.
points: Counter-movements arise to defend the status quo against a social movement, e.g. the Dharma Sabha, which petitioned the British against the law banning sati.
Movements use many methods of protest: marches, dharnas, hunger strikes, petitions, public meetings, and cultural forms like songs, poetry and street plays.
Gandhi's use of satyagraha, non-violent resistance, made methods like fasting and civil disobedience famous.
Early sociologists saw social movements as threats to social order. Later sociologists saw them as important sources of social change and of new ideas.

example.q: Identify the movement and counter-movement: reformers demand an end to sati; orthodox groups petition to keep it.
steps: Reformers seeking change: the social movement.
Orthodox groups defending the existing practice: the counter-movement (e.g. the Dharma Sabha).
example.answer: Anti-sati campaign versus the Dharma Sabha counter-movement.

learn.reallife: Street plays (nukkad nataks) by college groups on topics like dowry or the environment are a modern cultural method of protest.

options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A

A is true, but R is false

quiz.explain: Defenders of existing arrangements mobilise against change.

quiz.q: Gandhi made which method of protest famous?
options: Armed rebellion

quiz.explain: Satyagraha used non-violent resistance.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Do all movements go smoothly? And how do people protest?'
teach.praise: Movements face counter-movements like the Dharma Sabha, and use marches, dharnas, fasts, songs and plays. Sociologists now see them as engines of change!
teach.nudge: But what is a counter-movement, and what methods do movements use?

learn.hook: Millions of people feel cheated by the system, yet most never join a movement. Why do some grievances become movements while others stay silent?
points: Theory of relative deprivation: social conflict arises when a group feels it is worse off than others; this sense of deprivation can drive collective protest.
Limits: feelings of deprivation are not enough to cause a movement; many deprived groups never mobilise. The theory also does not explain how movements organise.
Mancur Olson, 'The Logic of Collective Action' (1965): a movement is a sum of rational individuals pursuing self-interest; a person joins only if the gains outweigh the costs.
Resource mobilisation theory (John McCarthy and Mayer Zald): a movement's success depends on its ability to mobilise resources: leadership, organisational capacity, communication and networks.
Critique of resource mobilisation: movements can emerge and succeed even with limited resources, creating resources as they grow.

example.q: Compare how relative deprivation and resource mobilisation theories would explain a farmers' movement.
steps: Relative deprivation: farmers feel worse off than urban groups, which fuels anger.
Resource mobilisation: the movement grows because it has leaders, organisations, money and networks.
The first explains motivation; the second explains capacity to act.
example.answer: Deprivation explains grievances; resource mobilisation explains organisation and success.

learn.reallife: Movements that use social media to raise funds, coordinate volunteers and spread messages are applying the logic of resource mobilisation.

quiz.explain: Resources and organisation are decisive.

options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A

options: Relative deprivation theory

quiz.mistake: Picks a theory about grievances or population

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why do some angry groups start movements while others don't?'
teach.praise: Deprivation gives the anger, Olson says people weigh costs and gains, and McCarthy and Zald say resources decide success. Critics add movements can create resources!
teach.nudge: But what do the three theories say, and what are their limits?

learn.hook: One movement asks people to change their inner selves; another asks for a new law; a third aims to overthrow the whole system. Sociologists classify movements by how deep a change they seek.
points: Redemptive movements aim to change the inner consciousness and actions of individuals. Example: the Ezhava movement in Kerala led by Narayana Guru, which changed religious practices and self-perception.

Reformist movements aim to change existing social and political arrangements through gradual, step-by-step means. Examples: the campaign for linguistic reorganisation of states, and the Right to Information campaign.
Revolutionary movements aim to radically transform social relations, often by seizing state power. Examples: the Bolshevik revolution in Russia and the Naxalite movement in India.
Many movements combine elements of more than one type and can change over time.

example.q: Classify: (a) a movement asking followers to give up liquor and adopt new forms of worship; (b) a campaign for a new law; (c) a movement aiming to overthrow the state.
steps: (a) Changing individuals' inner lives: redemptive.
(b) Gradual change in arrangements: reformist.
(c) Radical transformation through state power: revolutionary.
example.answer: (a) redemptive; (b) reformist; (c) revolutionary.

learn.hook: In the 1930s, most movements were about class and freedom from colonial rule. By the 1970s, people were also marching for forests, women's rights and human rights. Sociologists called these 'new' social movements.
points: 'Old' social movements were organised mainly around class (workers, peasants) and anti-colonial goals, and worked through political parties. Their focus was redistribution of power and resources.

'New' social movements, prominent from the 1970s, focus on quality of life, environment, identity and human rights, e.g. women's, environmental and anti-nuclear movements. They often work outside political parties.
New movements are often international in reach and are less about seizing state power than about changing values and policies.

In India, old and new movements overlap: issues of identity (caste, tribe, gender) are often combined with issues of resources (land, forests, wages). Chipko, for example, was both ecological and economic.

example.q: Why is it hard to separate 'old' and 'new' movements in India?
steps: Indian movements about environment or identity also involve livelihoods and resources.
E.g. tribal movements combine identity with land and forest rights.
So class issues and new issues are intertwined.
example.answer: Identity and resource issues are usually combined in Indian movements.

learn.reallife: Global campaigns on climate change that connect students across countries are typical 'new' social movements.

learn.hook: In the early 1970s, when contractors arrived to cut trees in the Himalayan villages of present-day Uttarakhand, village women hugged the trees and refused to let go. 'Chipko' means 'to hug' or 'to stick'.
points: Development has costs for nature and people: deforestation, large dams, mining and displacement of communities.
The Chipko movement in the Himalayan region (now Uttarakhand) began in the early 1970s; villagers, especially women, hugged trees to stop them being cut by contractors.

Chipko combined ecological concerns (protecting forests), economic concerns (forests gave fuel, fodder and livelihoods for subsistence) and political concerns (resentment against a distant state and outside contractors, and demand for local control).
Ecological movements question the dominant model of development that treats nature only as a resource for industry and cities.

example.q: Explain why Chipko is called both an ecological and an economic movement.
steps: Ecological: it protected forests from felling.
Economic: villagers depended on forests for fuel, fodder and water for subsistence.
Losing forests threatened their livelihood, so saving trees meant saving livelihoods.
example.answer: Forests were both an ecosystem and the villagers' economic base.

learn.reallife: Chipko inspired the Appiko movement in Karnataka, where villagers hugged trees in the Western Ghats in the 1980s.

topics.title: Peasant movements and new farmers' movements

learn.hook: In 1917 Gandhi went to Champaran in Bihar, where peasants were forced to grow indigo. In 1928, peasants of Bardoli in Gujarat refused to pay increased revenue. Peasant struggles shaped India's freedom movement.
points: Colonial peasant movements: the Bengal indigo revolt (1859-62), the Deccan riots (1875), Champaran satyagraha (1917) and Bardoli satyagraha (1928).
The All India Kisan Sabha was formed in 1936 to organise peasants on issues like land revenue, rents and debt.

Post-war struggles: Tebhaga (Bengal, 1946-47), where sharecroppers demanded two-thirds of the crop; Telangana (1946-51) against feudal landlords in Hyderabad state; and Naxalbari (West Bengal, 1967), an armed peasant uprising.

New farmers' movements from the 1970s, in Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and elsewhere, were led by market-oriented farmers. Their issues were prices, cost of inputs and subsidies; they were regionally organised and largely non-party, using methods like road and rail blockades.

example.q: How did new farmers' movements differ from earlier peasant movements?
steps: Earlier movements: mainly tenants and poor peasants against landlords and the colonial state over rent and revenue.
New farmers' movements: market-oriented farmers against the state over prices, inputs and subsidies.
New movements were regional and non-party.
example.answer: They shifted from land and rent to prices and inputs, and from party links to non-party organisation.

learn.reallife: Farmers' groups blocking highways for better minimum support prices continue the methods of the new farmers' movements.

learn.hook: In 1974, about 17 lakh railway workers went on strike, bringing India's lifeline to a halt. The workers' movement had come a long way since the first mill strikes of the 19th century.
points: Early workers' protests began with strikes in textile mills and other factories in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
The Madras Labour Union, one of India's first trade unions, was formed in 1918. The All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) was formed in 1920.
After independence, unions split along party lines, with different political parties having their own trade union wings.
The railway strike of 1974 was one of the largest strikes in India's history.
With the growth of the informal sector and contract work, trade unions have weakened, since such workers are hard to organise.

example.q: Why did trade unions split after independence?
steps: Different political parties formed their own union federations.
Unions became linked to party ideologies.
Workers were divided along party lines.
example.answer: Splits followed party lines as parties built union wings.

learn.hook: For Dalit movements, the struggle has always been about more than wages. It is about being treated as an equal human being: entering temples, drawing water from common wells and living with dignity.
points: The Dalit movement is a struggle for recognition as fellow human beings: for dignity, equality and self-respect, not just economic gains.
Examples: the Satnami movement (Chhattisgarh), the Adi-Dharma movement (Punjab), the Mahar movement (Maharashtra), and the political and social movement led by B.R. Ambedkar.
The Dalit Panthers (1970s) and a rich Dalit literature in Marathi and other languages became powerful forms of assertion.
Backward class and caste movements, especially non-Brahmin movements in the south (e.g. in Tamil Nadu), challenged Brahmin dominance in education, jobs and politics.
Some upper-caste groups have responded with a sense of 'reverse discrimination' and anti-reservation protests, e.g. after the Mandal recommendations were implemented in 1990.

example.q: Why is the Dalit movement described as a struggle for recognition, not just economic gain?
steps: Untouchability denied Dalits basic human dignity.
Their demands included temple entry, equal access to water and an end to humiliation.
So the struggle was about self-respect and equality as human beings.
example.answer: Because its core demand is dignity and equal humanity.

learn.reallife: Ambedkar's Mahad satyagraha of 1927, asserting Dalits' right to draw water from a public tank, is a landmark of the struggle for dignity.

learn.hook: In 1899-1900, Birsa Munda led an uprising, the Ulgulan, against British officials, landlords and moneylenders in the Chota Nagpur region. A century later, in 2000, the state of Jharkhand was born.
points: Tribal movements have been concentrated in the central Indian 'tribal belt' (e.g. the Chota Nagpur and Santhal Parganas regions of Jharkhand) and in the North-East.
The Jharkhand movement: a long struggle against dikus (outsiders: moneylenders, traders, migrant settlers) and against land loss; it led to the creation of Jharkhand state in 2000.
Birsa Munda, who led a revolt against the British and dikus, became an enduring symbol of tribal resistance.
Key issues: land alienation, forest rights, displacement by mining and dams, and protection of cultural identity.
North-East movements focus on ethnic identity, autonomy and land rights.

steps: Dikus were outsiders: moneylenders, traders and settlers.
They took tribal land through debt and fraud.
Opposing them meant defending land and identity.
example.answer: Dikus were seen as responsible for land loss and exploitation.

learn.hook: In 1974, a government committee's report, 'Towards Equality', revealed how far Indian women still lagged behind men despite constitutional promises. It sparked a new wave of the women's movement.
points: Early 20th-century women's organisations: the Women's India Association (1917), the All India Women's Conference (1926) and the National Council of Women in India (1925).
Women participated actively in the freedom struggle, and also in peasant and tribal movements such as Tebhaga and Telangana.

The movement revived in the 1970s after the 'Towards Equality' report (1974) of the Committee on the Status of Women in India. New autonomous women's groups, independent of political parties, emerged.
Campaigns against custodial rape (the Mathura case), dowry deaths and violence against women led to legal reforms in the 1980s.
The focus shifted from 'welfare' to 'rights' and 'empowerment', and the movement increasingly recognised the diverse issues of Dalit, tribal and working-class women.

example.q: Trace the shift in focus of the women's movement.
steps: Early phase: women's organisations, education and participation in the national movement.
1970s onward: autonomous groups, campaigns on violence, custodial rape and dowry.
Later: from welfare to rights and empowerment, recognising diverse women's issues.
example.answer: From welfare and reform to rights, empowerment and diversity.

learn.reallife: Campaigns after the Mathura case led to changes in rape law in 1983, a landmark showing how the movement shaped legislation.

All India Women's Conference (1926)
'Towards Equality' report (1974)
Legal reforms on violence (1980s)

games.title: Women's movement
items: The Women's India Association was formed in 1917.
It was one of the earliest women's organisations.
Women did not take part in peasant movements.
They took part in Tebhaga and Telangana.
'Towards Equality' was published in 1974.
It revived the women's movement.
The Mathura case was about custodial rape.
It sparked legal reform.
The movement shifted from rights to welfare.
It shifted from welfare to rights and empowerment.

quiz.q: The Women's India Association was formed in:
quiz.explain: It was founded in 1917.
quiz.mistake: Confuses with AIWC or the 1974 report

quiz.q: The All India Women's Conference was founded in:
quiz.explain: AIWC was founded in 1926.

quiz.q: The 'Towards Equality' report (1974) is significant because it:
options: Revived the women's movement
Abolished sati
Created linguistic states
Started the Green Revolution
quiz.explain: It showed the gap between promises and reality.

quiz.q: The Mathura case led to campaigns against:
options: Child labour in mines
Custodial rape
Indigo cultivation
Land ceiling evasion
quiz.explain: It sparked legal reform on custodial rape.

quiz.q: Women participated in which peasant movements?
options: Chipko and Appiko only
Bombay textile strike only
Tebhaga and Telangana
Champaran only
quiz.explain: Women were active in Tebhaga and Telangana.

quiz.q: The focus of the women's movement shifted from:
options: Rights to welfare and charity
Welfare to rights and empowerment
Empowerment to charity alone
Politics to silence and retreat
quiz.explain: The movement now stresses rights.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Autonomous women's groups emerged in the 1970s.
Reason (R): They were independent of political parties.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: 'Autonomous' means party-independent; that is what made them distinct.

quiz.q: Which is a feature of the women's movement in recent decades?
options: Ignoring all of the real differences among women
Focusing only on the concerns of rich urban women
Opposing every kind of legal reform for women's rights
Recognising issues of Dalit, tribal and working women
quiz.explain: Diversity of women's experience is recognised.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How has the women's movement changed over the last century?'
teach.praise: From WIA (1917) and AIWC (1926) to the 1974 report, autonomous groups, campaigns against violence and a shift from welfare to rights!
teach.nudge: But what were the phases and main issues of the women's movement?
